statement: A florist makes bouquets from roses, lilies and tulips. Let $r$, $l$ and $t$ be the numbers of roses, lilies and tulips in one bouquet. The bouquet has $10$ flowers in total. The flowers cost $2$ dollars per rose, $3$ dollars per lily and $1$ dollar per tulip, and the bouquet costs $18$ dollars in total. The number of roses plus twice the number of lilies, minus the number of tulips, is $3$. (a) Write down three equations for $r$, $l$ and $t$. [3] (b) Solve the system without a calculator, and state the number of each flower. [4]
markscheme: (a) $r+l+t=10$ [A1]; $2r+3l+t=18$ [A1]; $r+2l-t=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Subtract the first from the second: $r+2l=8$ [M1]; add the first and third: $2r+3l=13$ [M1]; $l=3$ and $r=2$ [A1]; $t=5$, so $2$ roses, $3$ lilies and $5$ tulips [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Eliminate $t$ first to get two equations in $r$ and $l$. Check the answer in all three original equations.

subtopic: Singular matrix with a parameter
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & k\\ 3 & 6\end{pmatrix}$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which $A$ is singular. [2] (b) For $k=1$, find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) For $k=1$, solve $A\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\ 9\end{pmatrix}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det A=12-3k$ [A1]; $=0\Rightarrow k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det A=9$ [A1]; $A^{-1}=\dfrac19\begin{pmatrix}6 & -1\\ -3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}7\\ 9\end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac19\begin{pmatrix}42-9\\ -21+18\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{11}{3}, \ y=-\dfrac13$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is $0$. The inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ is $\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}$.

subtopic: Simple and compound interest without a calculator
statement: A sum of $2000$ dollars is invested at an annual interest rate of $10\%$. (a) Find the value of the investment after $2$ years with simple interest and with interest compounded annually. [3] (b) Find the difference between the two values after $3$ years. [3]
markscheme: (a) Simple: $2000+2\times200=2400$ dollars [A1]; compound: $2000\times1.1^2$ [M1] $=2420$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) Simple: $2000+3\times200=2600$ [A1]; compound: $2000\times1.331=2662$ [A1]; difference $=62$ dollars [A1] [3 marks]
tips: With simple interest the interest is always $10\%$ of the original amount. With compound interest the amount is multiplied by $1.1$ each year.

subtopic: Car loan with extra monthly payments
statement: A car loan of $25000$ dollars has an annual interest rate of $6.6\%$ compounded monthly. The loan is repaid with equal payments at the end of each month over $5$ years. All money values are rounded to the nearest cent. (a) Find the monthly payment. [2] (b) Find the total interest paid over the $5$ years, using the rounded monthly payment. [2] (c) The borrower decides to pay $100$ dollars more each month, so $590.33$ dollars per month. Find the number of payments needed to repay the loan, with the last payment smaller. [3] (d) Find the last payment and the total interest saved compared with the original plan. Use the exact balance after $48$ payments and give money values to the nearest cent. [3]
markscheme: (a) $N=60$, $I\%=6.6$, $PV=25000$, $PMT$ unknown, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1]; $490.33$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (b) $60\times490.33=29419.80$ [M1]; interest $=4419.80$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve for $N$ with $PMT=-590.33$ [M1]; $N=48.3$ [A1]; so $49$ payments [A1] [3 marks] (d) Balance after $48$ payments plus one month's interest: last payment $=203.60$ dollars [A1]; total paid $=48\times590.33+203.60=28539.44$, interest $=3539.44$ [A1]; saving $=4419.80-3539.44=880.36$ dollars [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the finance solver for $N$ and for the payment. The final payment is the remaining balance plus one month of interest.

subtopic: Market share as a Markov chain
statement: Three phone brands A, B, C share a market. Each month, of the customers of A, $80\%$ stay with A, $12\%$ move to B and $8\%$ move to C. Of the customers of B, $10\%$ move to A, $75\%$ stay and $15\%$ move to C. Of the customers of C, $6\%$ move to A, $14\%$ move to B and $80\%$ stay. Initially the market shares of A, B, C are $20\%$, $50\%$ and $30\%$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$ in which each column gives the probabilities of moving from one brand to the three brands, and the initial state vector. [3] (b) Find the market shares after $3$ months, as percentages to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the long-term market shares, as percentages to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the first month in which the market share of A exceeds $27\%$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix}0.80 & 0.10 & 0.06\\ 0.12 & 0.75 & 0.14\\ 0.08 & 0.15 & 0.80\end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; initial state $\begin{pmatrix}0.2\\ 0.5\\ 0.3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $T^3\begin{pmatrix}0.2\\ 0.5\\ 0.3\end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; A: $25.8\%$ [A1]; B: $38.2\%$, C: $36.0\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $T\mathbf s=\mathbf s$ with the shares adding to $1$ (or a high power of $T$) [M1]; A: $28.4\%$ [A1]; B: $34.4\%$, C: $37.2\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Share of A after $n$ months: $22.8, 24.6, 25.8, 26.7, 27.2\ (\%)$ [M1]; $n=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The columns of the transition matrix each sum to $1$. The long-term state satisfies $T\mathbf s=\mathbf s$.

subtopic: A spiraling robot arm and complex multiplication
statement: The tip of a robot arm starts at the point $z_0=10$ in the complex plane (units are centimeters). At each step the arm is moved by multiplying its position by the complex number $q=0.9\,e^{i\pi/12}$, so $z_{n+1}=q\,z_n$. (a) State the modulus and argument of $q$ and describe the effect of one step on the position of the tip. [3] (b) Find the position $z_8$ of the tip after $8$ steps in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the smallest $n$ for which the tip is less than $0.5$ cm from the origin. [3] (d) Find the first $n$ for which $z_n$ is a negative real number. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|q|=0.9$ [A1]; $\arg q=\dfrac\pi{12}$ [A1]; each step rotates the tip by $\dfrac\pi{12}$ ($15^\circ$) anticlockwise about the origin and shrinks its distance from the origin by a factor $0.9$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z_8=10q^8=10\times0.9^8e^{i2\pi/3}$ [M1]; $|z_8|=4.30$ [A1]; $z_8=-2.15+3.73i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $10\times0.9^n\lt0.5$ [M1]; $n\gt\dfrac{\ln0.05}{\ln0.9}=28.4$ [A1]; $n=29$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Need $\dfrac{n\pi}{12}=\pi+2k\pi$ [M1]; $n=12$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiplication by $re^{i\theta}$ scales by $r$ and rotates by $\theta$. Use $z_n=z_0q^n$.

subtopic: Star magnitudes and a logarithmic scale
statement: The apparent magnitude $m$ of a star is related to its brightness $b$ by $m=m_0-2.5\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{b}{b_0}\right)$, where $m_0$ and $b_0$ are constants. A smaller magnitude means a brighter star. (a) Show that a star that is $100$ times brighter than another star has a magnitude that is $5$ lower. [2] (b) Star X has magnitude $1.2$ and star Y has magnitude $4.6$. Find how many times brighter star X is than star Y, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Two identical stars each have magnitude $3.0$ and appear as one object. Their brightnesses add. Find the combined magnitude to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Brightnesses add, but magnitudes do not. Convert to brightness, add, then convert back.

subtopic: Bounds on a calculated density
statement: A metal block has mass $152$ g, measured to the nearest gram, and volume $19.3\ \text{cm}^3$, measured to the nearest $0.1\ \text{cm}^3$. Its density is mass divided by volume. (a) Write down the lower and upper bounds for the mass and for the volume. [2] (b) Calculate the density using the measured values, and find the lower and upper bounds for the density. Give your answers to 4 significant figures. [4] (c) Find the greatest possible percentage error in the calculated density, to 2 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Mass: $151.5\le m\lt152.5$ [A1]; volume: $19.25\le V\lt19.35$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Density $=\dfrac{152}{19.3}=7.876\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ [A1]; lower bound $=\dfrac{151.5}{19.35}$ [M1] $=7.829$ [A1]; upper bound $=\dfrac{152.5}{19.25}=7.922$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Greater deviation is above: $\dfrac{7.922-7.876}{7.876}\times100$ [M1] $=0.59\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide the largest mass by the smallest volume for the upper bound and the smallest mass by the largest volume for the lower bound.

subtopic: Cross rates and a currency cycle
statement: A bank quotes these exchange rates: $1$ USD buys $0.92$ EUR; $1$ EUR buys $0.85$ GBP; $1$ GBP buys $1.30$ USD. A trader converts USD to EUR, then EUR to GBP, then GBP back to USD. (a) Starting with $10000$ USD, find how many USD the trader has after the three conversions, if there are no fees. [3] (b) Find the percentage gain from one cycle and the amount after $5$ cycles, to the nearest dollar. [3] (c) Each conversion carries a fee of $0.1\%$ of the amount being converted. Find the amount after one cycle, to the nearest cent, and the percentage gain. [3]
tips: Multiply the three rates to get the factor for one complete cycle. A fee of $0.1\%$ multiplies the amount by $0.999$.

subtopic: Two age groups: matrix model with eigenvalues
statement: A population has juveniles $j_n$ and adults $a_n$ in year $n$ (in hundreds). Each year, $j_{n+1}=1.2a_n$ and $a_{n+1}=0.5j_n+0.8a_n$. Let $\mathbf x_n=\begin{pmatrix}j_n\\ a_n\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathbf x_{n+1}=L\mathbf x_n$. Initially $j_0=100$ and $a_0=200$. (a) Write down the matrix $L$ and find $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2$. [3] (b) Find the eigenvalues of $L$, to 3 significant figures. State which one describes the long-term growth. [3] (c) Find an eigenvector for the larger eigenvalue and hence the long-term ratio of juveniles to adults, to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Use your calculator to find $\mathbf x_{10}$ and check that $\dfrac{j_{10}}{a_{10}}$ is close to your answer to part (c). [2]
markscheme: (a) $L=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1.2\\ 0.5 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf x_1=\begin{pmatrix}240\\ 210\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf x_2=\begin{pmatrix}252\\ 288\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda^2-0.8\lambda-0.6=0$ [M1]; $\lambda=1.27$ and $\lambda=-0.472$ [A1]; the larger in magnitude, $1.27$, gives long-term growth of $27\%$ per year [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-\lambda j+1.2a=0$ with $\lambda=1.2718$ [M1]; $j:a=1.2:1.2718$ [A1]; ratio $=0.944$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf x_{10}=\begin{pmatrix}1820\\ 1930\end{pmatrix}$ (3 s.f.) [A1]; $\dfrac{1823}{1932}=0.944$, which agrees [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The long-term behavior of $L^n\mathbf x_0$ is dominated by the eigenvalue of largest magnitude.

subtopic: Complex numbers as rotation-scaling matrices
statement: This question links complex numbers and $2\times2$ matrices. To each complex number $z=a+bi$ associate the matrix $M_z=\begin{pmatrix}a & -b\\ b & a\end{pmatrix}$. A point $(x, y)$ is associated with the complex number $x+yi$ and the vector $\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $M_z\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}$ is the vector associated with $z(x+yi)$. [3] (b) Let $z=\sqrt3+i$. Write down $M_z$, find $\det M_z$ and show that $\det M_z=|z|^2$. [3] (c) Write $z=\sqrt3+i$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ and explain, in terms of a transformation of the plane, what $M_z$ does to a point. [3] (d) Find the exact value of $M_z^6$ and explain the answer geometrically. [3] (e) The unit square with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(0, 1)$ is transformed by $M_z$. Find the area of the image and explain why it is $|z|^2$. [3] (f) Find the eigenvalues of $M_z$ in the form $p+qi$ and describe their connection with $z$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $M_z\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}ax-by\\ bx+ay\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $(a+bi)(x+yi)=(ax-by)+(bx+ay)i$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $M_z=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3 & -1\\ 1 & \sqrt3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\det M_z=3+1=4$ [M1]; $|z|^2=3+1=4$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $r=2$, $\theta=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1][A1]; $M_z$ rotates every point by $\dfrac\pi6$ anticlockwise about the origin and enlarges it by factor $2$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $z^6=2^6\left(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi\right)=-64$ [M1]; $M_z^6=\begin{pmatrix}-64 & 0\\ 0 & -64\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; six rotations of $\dfrac\pi6$ make a half turn, and six enlargements of factor $2$ give factor $64$ [R1] [3 marks] (e) Area scale factor $=|\det M_z|$ [M1]; image area $=4$ [A1]; an enlargement of factor $2$ multiplies area by $2^2=4$ and a rotation does not change area [R1] [3 marks] (f) $\det\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3-\lambda & -1\\ 1 & \sqrt3-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=\left(\sqrt3-\lambda\right)^2+1=0$ [M1]; $\lambda=\sqrt3\pm i$ [A1]; the eigenvalues are $z$ and its conjugate $\bar z$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiplying by a complex number $re^{i\theta}$ rotates by $\theta$ and scales by $r$. The matrix $M_z$ encodes the same transformation.

subtopic: Regular tetrahedron: height and volume
statement: A regular tetrahedron has four equilateral triangle faces, each with edge length $6$ cm. Its base is triangle $ABC$ and its apex is $D$. Let $M$ be the centroid of the base, which is directly below $D$. (a) Show that $AM=2\sqrt3$ cm. [3] (b) Find the exact height $DM$ of the tetrahedron. [2] (c) Find the exact volume of the tetrahedron. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height of the base triangle $=6\sin60^\circ=3\sqrt3$ [A1]; the centroid divides a median in the ratio $2:1$, so $AM=\dfrac23\times3\sqrt3$ [M1] $=2\sqrt3$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $DM^2=6^2-(2\sqrt3)^2=36-12=24$ [M1]; $DM=2\sqrt6$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Base area $=\dfrac12\times6\times6\sin60^\circ=9\sqrt3$ [A1]; $V=\dfrac13\times9\sqrt3\times2\sqrt6$ [M1]; $=6\sqrt{18}=18\sqrt2\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In an equilateral triangle the centroid is $\frac23$ of the way along each median from a vertex.

subtopic: Cone inscribed in a sphere
statement: A cone is inscribed in a sphere of radius $5$ cm: the apex of the cone and the circumference of its base lie on the sphere, and the base is at distance $3$ cm from the center of the sphere, on the opposite side from the apex. The height of the cone is therefore $8$ cm. (a) Show that the radius of the base of the cone is $4$ cm. [2] (b) Find the exact volume of the cone and of the sphere. [3] (c) Find the fraction of the volume of the sphere that is occupied by the cone, in lowest terms. [2]
markscheme: (a) The radius $r$ of the base satisfies $r^2+3^2=5^2$ [M1]; $r=4$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) Cone: $\dfrac13\pi\times16\times8=\dfrac{128\pi}{3}$ [A1]; sphere: $\dfrac43\pi\times125=\dfrac{500\pi}{3}$ [A1][A1] ($\text{cm}^3$) [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{128}{500}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{32}{125}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use Pythagoras in the right triangle formed by the sphere's radius, the distance $3$ and the base radius.

subtopic: Cylinder inside a cone using similar triangles
statement: A solid cone has base radius $6$ cm and height $9$ cm. A cylinder of radius $3$ cm stands with its base on the base of the cone and its upper circular edge touching the sloping surface of the cone, so that the axes of the two solids coincide. (a) Find the height of the cylinder. [3] (b) Find the exact volume of the cylinder, and show that it is $\dfrac{3}{8}$ of the volume of the cone. [4]
markscheme: (a) By similar triangles, the small cone above the cylinder has radius $3$ and so height $\dfrac{3}{6}\times9=4.5$ [M1][A1]; cylinder height $=9-4.5=4.5$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) Cylinder: $\pi\times3^2\times4.5=40.5\pi=\dfrac{81\pi}{2}$ [A1]; cone: $\dfrac13\pi\times36\times9=108\pi$ [A1]; ratio $=\dfrac{81/2}{108}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac38$ [AG] [4 marks]
tips: The part of the cone above the cylinder is a smaller cone similar to the whole cone.

subtopic: Arc and chord on a sphere
statement: Treat the Earth as a sphere of radius $6400$ km. Two points P and Q lie on the equator, with the angle $POQ=60^\circ$ at the center O of the Earth. (a) Find the exact length of the arc PQ along the equator. [2] (b) Find the exact straight-line distance PQ through the Earth, and explain why triangle $OPQ$ is equilateral. [3] (c) Write down an exact expression for how much longer the arc is than the chord. [2]
markscheme: (a) Arc $=\dfrac{60}{360}\times2\pi\times6400$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6400\pi}{3}$ km [A1] [2 marks] (b) $OP=OQ=6400$ and $\angle POQ=60^\circ$, so the other two angles are equal and sum to $120^\circ$, giving $60^\circ$ each [R1]; so the triangle is equilateral [A1]; $PQ=6400$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) Difference $=\dfrac{6400\pi}{3}-6400$ [M1] $=6400\left(\dfrac\pi3-1\right)$ km [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A triangle with two equal sides and a $60^\circ$ angle between them is equilateral.

subtopic: Regular hexagonal pyramid
statement: A right pyramid has a regular hexagonal base of side $4$ cm and a vertical height of $6$ cm. (a) Find the exact area of the base. [2] (b) Find the exact volume of the pyramid. [2] (c) Find the exact length of a sloping edge from a vertex of the base to the apex. [2] (d) Find the exact total surface area of the pyramid. [3]
markscheme: (a) A regular hexagon consists of $6$ equilateral triangles of side $4$ [M1]; area $=6\times\dfrac12\times4\times4\sin60^\circ=24\sqrt3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac13\times24\sqrt3\times6$ [M1] $=48\sqrt3\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The distance from the center of the hexagon to a vertex is $4$ [M1]; $\sqrt{4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (d) Distance from center to the midpoint of a base edge $=4\sin60^\circ=2\sqrt3$ [A1]; slant height $=\sqrt{6^2+12}=4\sqrt3$ [A1]; total $=24\sqrt3+6\times\dfrac12\times4\times4\sqrt3=72\sqrt3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The distance from the center of a regular hexagon to each vertex equals its side length.

subtopic: Spheres packed in a cube
statement: Eight identical solid spheres are packed in a cube of side $12$ cm, in two layers of four, so that each sphere touches the faces of the cube nearest to it and touches its neighboring spheres. (a) Find the radius of each sphere. [1] (b) Find the exact total volume of the eight spheres. [2] (c) Show that the fraction of the cube that is empty is $1-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) The cube side holds two sphere diameters: $4r=12$, so $r=3$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) $8\times\dfrac43\pi\times3^3$ [M1] $=288\pi\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Cube volume $=1728$ [A1]; filled fraction $=\dfrac{288\pi}{1728}=\dfrac\pi6$ [M1]; empty fraction $=1-\dfrac\pi6$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Along one edge of the cube there are two sphere diameters.

subtopic: Shortest path across the surface of a cuboid
statement: A cuboid has dimensions $3$ cm by $4$ cm by $12$ cm. An ant walks along the surface from one corner A to the opposite corner G. (a) Show that the straight-line distance through the cuboid from A to G is $13$ cm. [2] (b) An ant must stay on the surface. By unfolding two adjacent faces, find the lengths of three possible paths and write down the exact length of the shortest. [5]
markscheme: (a) $AG^2=3^2+4^2+12^2$ [M1]; $=169$, so $AG=13$ cm [AG] [2 marks] (b) Unfold so that the path crosses a common edge and form right triangles [M1]; the legs are $(3+4, 12)$ giving $\sqrt{49+144}=\sqrt{193}$ [A1]; $(3+12, 4)$ giving $\sqrt{225+16}=\sqrt{241}$ [A1]; $(4+12, 3)$ giving $\sqrt{256+9}=\sqrt{265}$ [A1]; shortest $=\sqrt{193}$ cm [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Unfold the two faces the path crosses into one flat rectangle, and the shortest path is the straight line across it.

subtopic: Face diagonals and space diagonal of a cube
statement: A cube $ABCDEFGH$ has side $6$ cm, with $ABCD$ the base, $EFGH$ the top face, and $AE$, $BF$, $CG$, $DH$ vertical edges. (a) Show that triangle $ACF$ is equilateral and write down the angle $CAF$. [3] (b) Find the exact tangent of the angle between the space diagonal $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [3] (c) Find the exact value of $\cos\angle BAG$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{36+36}=6\sqrt2$ [A1]; $AF=6\sqrt2$ and $CF=6\sqrt2$ (each is a face diagonal) [A1]; so $ACF$ is equilateral and $\angle CAF=60^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Projection of $AG$ onto the base is $AC=6\sqrt2$ [A1]; $CG=6$ [A1]; $\tan\theta=\dfrac{6}{6\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $AG=6\sqrt3$ and $AB=6$, triangle $ABG$ has a right angle at $B$ [M1]; $\cos\angle BAG=\dfrac{6}{6\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Every face diagonal of a cube has length $\text{side}\times\sqrt2$.

subtopic: Lampshade as a frustum and its flat pattern
statement: A lampshade is the curved surface of a frustum of a cone with top radius $8$ cm, bottom radius $14$ cm and slant height $18$ cm (open at both ends). (a) Find the perpendicular height of the lampshade, to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the area of the material needed for the curved surface, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) The frustum is cut from a complete cone. Show that the slant height of the complete cone is $42$ cm and that of the removed small cone is $24$ cm. [3] (d) The curved surface is made from a flat piece shaped as part of a ring between two circular arcs about the same center. Find the angle of this ring sector, in degrees. [2]
markscheme: (a) $h=\sqrt{18^2-(14-8)^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{288}=17.0$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\pi(R+r)\times\ell=\pi\times22\times18$ [M1] $=1240\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Similar cones: $\dfrac{\ell_1}{8}=\dfrac{\ell_1+18}{14}$ [M1]; $14\ell_1=8\ell_1+144$ [A1]; $\ell_1=24$, so the whole cone has slant height $42$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) Arc of the inner edge $=2\pi\times8=\ell_1\theta=24\theta$ [M1]; $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians $=120^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Cones cut by a plane parallel to the base are similar. The arc length of the flat pattern equals the circumference of the circle it forms.

subtopic: Distance between two ships seen from a lighthouse
statement: The lamp of a lighthouse is $60$ m above sea level. From the lamp, ship A is seen on a bearing of $040^\circ$ at an angle of depression of $5^\circ$, and ship B on a bearing of $100^\circ$ at an angle of depression of $3^\circ$. Treat the sea as flat. (a) Find the horizontal distance from the base of the lighthouse to each ship, to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the distance between the two ships, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the straight-line distance from the lamp to ship B, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d_A=\dfrac{60}{\tan5^\circ}$ [M1] $=686$ m [A1]; $d_B=\dfrac{60}{\tan3^\circ}$ [M1] $=1140$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) Angle at the base $=100^\circ-40^\circ=60^\circ$ [A1]; $AB^2=d_A^2+d_B^2-2d_Ad_B\cos60^\circ$ [M1]; $AB=998$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sqrt{1144.87^2+60^2}$ [M1] $=1150$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Draw a right triangle for each ship with the lighthouse height as one side, and then work in the horizontal plane with the angle between the bearings.

subtopic: A hip roof
statement: A hip roof covers a rectangular building $12$ m long and $8$ m wide. The roof has a horizontal ridge $4$ m long, centered above the building and parallel to the long sides, at a height of $3$ m above the top of the walls. Two roof faces are trapeziums with the ridge as the shorter parallel side; the other two are triangles at the ends. (a) Show that each trapezium face has area $40\ \text{m}^2$. [3] (b) Find the total roof area. [3] (c) Find the angle that a long roof face makes with the horizontal, to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) A hip is the sloping edge from a corner of the building to the nearer end of the ridge. Find the angle between a hip and the horizontal, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Horizontal distance from a long wall to the ridge $=4$ m, rise $=3$ m, so slant height $=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ m [M1][A1]; area $=\dfrac12(12+4)\times5=40$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) End face: base $8$, horizontal distance from end wall to ridge end $=\dfrac{12-4}{2}=4$, slant height $5$ [M1]; area $=\dfrac12\times8\times5=20$ [A1]; total $=2\times40+2\times20=120\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac34$ [M1]; $\theta=36.9^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Horizontal distance from a corner to the nearer end of the ridge $=\sqrt{4^2+4^2}=4\sqrt2$ [A1]; $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{3}{4\sqrt2}$ [M1]; $\alpha=27.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Work out where each face's slant height comes from by drawing a vertical cross-section perpendicular to the edge of that face.

subtopic: A barrel modeled by two frustums
statement: A barrel is modeled as two identical frustums of cones joined at their wider circular faces. Each frustum has a height of $25$ cm, a wider radius of $20$ cm and a narrower radius of $15$ cm. (a) Find the volume of one frustum, as the difference of two cones, to 3 significant figures. Use similar triangles for the height of the removed top. [4] (b) Find the capacity of the barrel in liters, to 3 significant figures, using the unrounded frustum volume. [2] (c) A cylinder of radius $20$ cm and height $50$ cm has a larger volume. Find the percentage of the cylinder's volume filled by the barrel model, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Removed small cone has height $x$ with $\dfrac{x}{15}=\dfrac{x+25}{20}$ [M1]; $x=75$ [A1]; $\dfrac13\pi\times20^2\times100-\dfrac13\pi\times15^2\times75$ [M1]; $=24200\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2\times24216=48433$ [M1]; $48.4$ liters [A1] [2 marks] (c) Cylinder $=\pi\times400\times50=62832\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1]; $\dfrac{48433}{62832}=77.1\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The formula $V=\frac{\pi h}{3}\left(R^2+Rr+r^2\right)$ for a frustum gives the same value.

subtopic: Largest sphere inside a cone
statement: A solid cone has base radius $5$ cm and perpendicular height $12$ cm. A sphere is placed inside the cone so that it touches the base and the sloping surface all the way around. (a) Find the slant height of the cone. [1] (b) Consider a vertical cross-section through the axis, which is an isosceles triangle with an inscribed circle. Show that the radius of the sphere is $\dfrac{10}{3}$ cm. [4] (c) Find the volume of the sphere and the percentage of the volume of the cone that it occupies, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) Area of the cross-section triangle $=\dfrac12\times10\times12=60$ [A1]; perimeter $=13+13+10=36$ [A1]; inradius $=\dfrac{2\times\text{area}}{\text{perimeter}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{120}{36}=\dfrac{10}{3}$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) Sphere: $\dfrac43\pi\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^3=155\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1]; cone: $\dfrac13\pi\times25\times12=314\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1]; percentage $=49.4\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The inscribed circle of a triangle has radius $\dfrac{2\times\text{area}}{\text{perimeter}}$.

subtopic: Water trough with a trapezoidal cross-section
statement: A water trough is a prism $3$ m long. Its cross-section is an isosceles trapezium that is $0.4$ m wide at the bottom, $0.8$ m wide at the top and $0.5$ m deep, with the narrower side at the bottom. (a) Find the capacity of the trough in liters. [3] (b) When the water in the trough has depth $h$ m, show that the width of the water surface is $0.4+0.8h$ m. [2] (c) Show that the volume of water is $V=1.2h^2+1.2h$ cubic meters, and find the depth of water when the trough is exactly half full, to 3 significant figures. [6] (d) Water is poured in at $9$ liters per minute. Find the time to fill the trough from empty, to the nearest minute. [2]
markscheme: (a) Area of cross-section $=\dfrac12(0.4+0.8)\times0.5=0.3\ \text{m}^2$ [M1][A1]; volume $=0.9\ \text{m}^3=900$ liters [A1] [3 marks] (b) The width increases by $0.4$ over a depth of $0.5$, i.e. at $0.8$ m per meter of depth [M1]; width $=0.4+0.8h$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Cross-section area $=\dfrac12\left(0.4+0.4+0.8h\right)h=0.4h+0.4h^2$ [M1][A1]; $V=3\times$ area $=1.2h+1.2h^2$ [AG]; half full: $1.2h^2+1.2h=0.45$ [M1]; $h=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{2.5}}{2}$ [A1]; $h=0.291$ m [A1] [6 marks] (d) $\dfrac{900}{9}$ [M1] $=100$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Find how the width of the water surface depends on the depth, then use the area of a trapezium for the cross-section.

subtopic: An octahedron inside a cube
statement: A cube has side $6$ cm. The centers of its six faces are joined to form a regular octahedron with eight equilateral triangular faces. Place the origin at the center of the cube with axes parallel to its edges, so the vertices of the octahedron are $(\pm3, 0, 0)$, $(0, \pm3, 0)$ and $(0, 0, \pm3)$. (a) Show that the edge length of the octahedron is $3\sqrt2$ cm. [2] (b) The octahedron is two identical square-based pyramids joined at their bases. Find the exact volume of the octahedron and the fraction of the cube that it occupies. [4] (c) Find the exact total surface area of the octahedron. [3] (d) A sphere inside the octahedron touches all eight faces. Using the fact that the volume of a solid whose faces are all at distance $r$ from an interior point is $\dfrac13r\times(\text{surface area})$, find the exact radius of this sphere and the exact fraction of the octahedron's volume that the sphere fills. [5] (e) The face with vertices $(3, 0, 0)$, $(0, 3, 0)$, $(0, 0, 3)$ has normal direction $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and the adjacent face with vertices $(3, 0, 0)$, $(0, 3, 0)$, $(0, 0, -3)$ has normal direction $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$, both pointing outward. Find the angle between these normals and hence the angle between the two faces measured inside the solid, to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) Distance between $(3, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 3, 0)$ [M1] is $\sqrt{9+9}=3\sqrt2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) Base square has side $3\sqrt2$, area $18$ [A1]; height of each pyramid $=3$ [A1]; $V=2\times\dfrac13\times18\times3=36\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1]; fraction $=\dfrac{36}{216}=\dfrac16$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) One face: $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times(3\sqrt2)^2=\dfrac{9\sqrt3}{2}$ [M1][A1]; total $=8\times\dfrac{9\sqrt3}{2}=36\sqrt3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $36=\dfrac13r\times36\sqrt3$ [M1]; $r=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$ cm [A1]; sphere volume $=\dfrac43\pi\left(\sqrt3\right)^3=4\sqrt3\pi$ [M1][A1]; fraction $=\dfrac{4\sqrt3\pi}{36}=\dfrac{\sqrt3\pi}{9}$ [A1] [5 marks] (e) $\cos\phi=\dfrac{1+1-1}{\sqrt3\times\sqrt3}=\dfrac13$ [M1][A1]; $\phi=70.5^\circ$ [A1]; the interior angle between the faces is $180^\circ-70.5^\circ=109^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The octahedron splits into two pyramids on a square base. For the sphere, split the solid into eight pyramids that meet at the center.

subtopic: Shortest paths on the surface of a cone and a cylinder
statement: An ant crawls over solid surfaces. A cone has base radius $3$ cm and slant height $12$ cm. When the curved surface is unrolled it forms a sector of a circle of radius $12$ cm. (a) Show that the angle of the sector is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians. [2] (b) Points P and Q are on the rim of the base at opposite ends of a diameter of the base. Explain why, in the unrolled sector, the angle between the straight lines from the apex to P and to Q is $\dfrac\pi4$, and find the length of the shortest path from P to Q over the curved surface, to 3 significant figures. [5] (c) Point R lies on the generator opposite to P, at distance $6$ cm from the apex. Find the shortest distance over the curved surface from P to R, to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) A cylinder has radius $2$ cm and height $10$ cm. An ant goes from a point on the bottom circle to the point on the top circle diametrically opposite, staying on the curved surface. Find the length of the shortest path, to 3 significant figures. [4] (e) Compare this with the path that goes straight up the side to the top circle and then across the top face along a diameter. [2]
markscheme: (a) Arc length of sector $=2\pi\times3=6\pi$ [M1]; angle $=\dfrac{6\pi}{12}=\dfrac\pi2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) Half of the rim is half of the arc of the sector, so the angle is half of $\dfrac\pi2$ [R1]; the shortest path is the straight chord of the sector [M1]; $PQ=2\times12\sin\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ [A1][A1]; $=9.18$ cm [A1] [5 marks] (c) Triangle with sides $12$ and $6$ and included angle $\dfrac\pi4$ [A1]; $PR^2=12^2+6^2-2\times12\times6\cos\dfrac\pi4$ [M1]; $PR=8.84$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (d) Unrolled, the curved surface is a rectangle $10$ by $4\pi$ [M1]; horizontal separation $=\pi\times2=2\pi$ [A1]; $\sqrt{10^2+(2\pi)^2}$ [M1]; $11.8$ cm [A1] [4 marks] (e) That path has length $10+4=14$ cm [A1]; it is longer than $11.8$ cm, so the path over the curved surface is shorter [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Unroll the curved surface into a flat shape; shortest paths on the surface become straight lines on the flat shape.

subtopic: Transforming a graph defined by its vertices
statement: The graph of $y=f(x)$ for $0\le x\le5$ is made of straight line segments joining the points $(0, 0)$, $(2, 4)$ and $(5, 1)$. (a) The graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from $y=f(x)$ by a horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ followed by a translation down by $1$ unit. Write down the coordinates of the three vertices of $y=g(x)$ and the domain of $g$. [4] (b) The graph of $y=h(x)$ is $y=-f(x-3)+2$. Write down the coordinates of the three vertices of $y=h(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=f(2x)-1$ [M1]; vertices $(0, -1)$ [A1], $(1, 3)$ [A1], $\left(\dfrac52, 0\right)$ [A1]; domain $0\le x\le\dfrac52$ (stated with the vertices) [4 marks] (b) $(3, 2)$ [A1]; $(5, -2)$ [A1]; $(8, 1)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac12$ halves every $x$-coordinate. Reflect in the $x$-axis by changing the sign of every $y$-coordinate.

subtopic: An absolute value graph from $y=|x|$
statement: Let $f(x)=|2x-4|+1$. (a) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=|x|$ onto the graph of $y=f(x)$, and write down the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(x)$. [4] (b) Solve $f(x)=x$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $|2x-4|=2|x-2|$ [M1]; vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ [A1]; translation by $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; vertex $(2, 1)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Case $x\ge2$: $2x-4+1=x\Rightarrow x=3$ [M1][A1]; case $x\lt2$: $-2x+4+1=x\Rightarrow x=\dfrac53$ [M1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: Factor out the coefficient of $x$ inside the modulus. Solve separately for the two cases of the absolute value.

subtopic: Translating a cubic
statement: The graph of $y=x^3$ is translated to give the graph of $y=g(x)$ with $g(x)=(x+2)^3-3$. (a) State the translation vector and the coordinates of the point of inflection of $y=g(x)$. [2] (b) Find the $y$-intercept and the exact $x$-intercept of the graph of $y=g(x)$. [3] (c) The graph of $y=g(x)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis. Write down the equation of the image. [1]
markscheme: (a) Translation $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ -3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; point of inflection $(-2, -3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $g(0)=8-3=5$ [A1]; $(x+2)^3=3$ [M1]; $x=\sqrt[3]{3}-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=3-(x+2)^3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Replace $x$ by $x+2$ to move the graph $2$ units to the left. A reflection in the $x$-axis changes the sign of the whole function.

subtopic: Undoing a sequence of transformations
statement: The graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $g(x)=3f(x-2)+1$. (a) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=f(x)$ onto the graph of $y=g(x)$, in the order in which they must be applied. [3] (b) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=g(x)$ back onto the graph of $y=f(x)$. [3] (c) The point $(5, 10)$ lies on the graph of $y=g(x)$. Write down the coordinates of the corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Translation by $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; vertical stretch with scale factor $3$ [A1]; translation by $\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Translation down by $1$ [A1]; vertical stretch with scale factor $\dfrac13$ [A1]; translation by $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x=5-2=3$ [A1]; $y=\dfrac{10-1}{3}=3$ so $(3, 3)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To undo a sequence of transformations, apply the inverse of each one in the reverse order.

subtopic: A vertical translation and the number of $x$-intercepts
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x$. (a) Find the $x$-intercepts of the graph of $y=f(x)$ and the coordinates of its vertex. [3] (b) The graph of $y=f(x)+k$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ translated vertically by $k$. Find the set of values of $k$ for which $y=f(x)+k$ has two distinct $x$-intercepts, exactly one $x$-intercept, and none. [4] (c) Write down the $x$-intercepts of the graph of $y=f(x-k)$ in terms of $k$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x(x-4)=0$ so $x=0$ and $x=4$ [A1]; vertex at $x=2$ [M1]; $(2, -4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Intercepts when $x^2-4x+k=0$, discriminant $=16-4k$ [M1]; two intercepts: $k\lt4$ [A1]; one intercept: $k=4$ [A1]; none: $k\gt4$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $x=k$ and $x=k+4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A horizontal translation changes where the graph crosses the $x$-axis; a vertical translation changes whether it does.

subtopic: Reflections and a translation of a line
statement: The line $L$ has equation $y=2x+1$. (a) Find the equations of the images of $L$ under a reflection in the $y$-axis, under a reflection in the $x$-axis, and under a reflection in both axes. [3] (b) $L$ is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix}3\\ -2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the equation of the image. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $L$ and its image under the reflection in the $x$-axis meet. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y$-axis: $y=-2x+1$ [A1]; $x$-axis: $y=-2x-1$ [A1]; both: $y=2x-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Replace $x$ by $x-3$ and subtract $2$: $y=2(x-3)+1-2$ [M1]; $y=2x-7$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2x+1=-2x-1$ [M1]; $x=-\dfrac12$, $y=0$, so $\left(-\dfrac12, 0\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Reflecting in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $-x$; reflecting in the $x$-axis replaces $y$ by $-y$.

subtopic: Writing a parabola from a sequence of transformations
statement: The graph of $y=x^2$ is stretched vertically with scale factor $3$, then reflected in the $x$-axis, and finally translated so that its vertex is at $(2, 5)$. (a) Find the equation of the resulting parabola in the form $y=a(x-h)^2+k$. [3] (b) Find the $y$-intercept and the exact $x$-intercepts. [4] (c) State the range of the function and its maximum value. [1]
markscheme: (a) After the stretch and reflection: $y=-3x^2$ [A1]; translation by $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 5\end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $y=-3(x-2)^2+5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y$-intercept: $-12+5=-7$ [A1]; $-3(x-2)^2+5=0$ [M1]; $(x-2)^2=\dfrac53$ [A1]; $x=2\pm\sqrt{\dfrac53}=2\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Range $y\le5$, maximum value $5$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Apply the transformations in the stated order. The vertex of $y=-3x^2$ is at the origin before the translation.

subtopic: Width of a transformed bell curve
statement: The intensity of a laser beam, in milliwatts per square centimeter, at distance $x$ cm along a line across the beam is $I(x)=6e^{-(x-3)^2/8}$. (a) The graph of $I$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=e^{-x^2}$ by a sequence of transformations. Describe them. [4] (b) Write down the maximum intensity and the value of $x$ where it occurs. [2] (c) The width of the beam is the distance between the two points where the intensity is half its maximum. Find this width, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Horizontal stretch with scale factor $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$ [A1][A1]; vertical stretch with scale factor $6$ [A1]; translation $3$ units to the right [A1] [4 marks] (b) $6$ mW cm$^{-2}$ [A1]; at $x=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $6e^{-(x-3)^2/8}=3$ [M1]; $x=0.645$ and $x=5.35$ [A1]; width $=4.71$ cm [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite $e^{-(x-3)^2/8}$ as $e^{-\left(\frac{x-3}{\sqrt8}\right)^2}$ to see the horizontal stretch. At half the maximum, $e^{-u}=\frac12$.

subtopic: A runner who starts late
statement: The distance in meters run by runner A in the first $t$ seconds of a race is $s(t)=10t-25\left(1-e^{-0.4t}\right)$. Runner B starts $2$ seconds later than A and covers $1.2$ times the distance that A would cover in the same running time, so B's distance at time $t$ is $b(t)=1.2\,s(t-2)$ for $t\ge2$. (a) Describe the transformations that map the graph of $y=s(t)$ onto the graph of $y=b(t)$. [2] (b) Find the distance run by A in the first $10$ seconds, and the distance run by B at $t=10$, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the time at which B catches A, and the distance from the start at that moment, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Translation $2$ units to the right [A1]; vertical stretch with scale factor $1.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s(10)=75.5$ m [A1]; $b(10)=1.2\,s(8)$ [M1] $=1.2\times56.0=67.2$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $b(t)=s(t)$ for $t\gt2$ [M1]; $t=14.4$ s [A1]; distance $=119$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Intersect the two graphs on your calculator, ignoring the start of the race where B has not yet started.

subtopic: Fitting a transformed exponential
statement: The number of followers $N$ (in thousands) of a channel $t$ months after launch is modeled by $N=a\cdot b^{t}+4$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants and $b\gt1$. The model passes through the points $(1, 7)$ and $(3, 16)$. (a) Find $a$ and $b$. [4] (b) State the equation of the horizontal asymptote and interpret the value $a+4$. [2] (c) Find the time at which the channel reaches $100$ thousand followers. [2] (d) Describe a transformation of the graph of $y=2^{t}$, other than a vertical stretch and translation, that gives the same curve as the graph of $y=1.5\times2^t$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $ab+4=7$ and $ab^3+4=16$ [M1]; $ab=3$, $ab^3=12$ [A1]; $b^2=4$, $b=2$ [A1]; $a=1.5$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $N=4$ [A1]; $a+4=5.5$ thousand is the model's number of followers at launch ($t=0$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1.5\times2^{t}+4=100$ [M1]; $2^t=64$, $t=6$ months [A1] [2 marks] (d) $1.5\times2^t=2^{t+\log_21.5}$ [M1]; translation $\log_21.5\approx0.585$ units to the left [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide the two equations (after subtracting $4$) to eliminate $a$.

subtopic: A reciprocal model and its intersection with a line
statement: A model of the form $y=\dfrac{a}{x-h}+k$ has vertical asymptote $x=2$ and horizontal asymptote $y=3$, and passes through the point $(4, 7)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $h$ and $k$. [3] (b) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps $y=\dfrac1x$ onto this graph. [3] (c) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the line $y=x$, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $h=2$, $k=3$ [A1]; $7=\dfrac{a}{2}+3$ [M1]; $a=8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Vertical stretch with scale factor $8$ [A1]; translation $2$ to the right [A1]; translation $3$ up [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $\dfrac{8}{x-2}+3=x$ [M1]; $x^2-5x-2=0$ [A1]; $x=5.37$ and $x=-0.372$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The asymptotes give the translation. Use the given point to find the vertical stretch.

subtopic: Changing the time unit
statement: The temperature in degrees Celsius of a cooling liquid $m$ minutes after it is poured is $T(m)=20+60e^{-0.05m}$. Let $g(h)$ be the temperature $h$ hours after it is poured, so $g(h)=T(60h)$. (a) Find $g(h)$ in the form $20+Ae^{-kh}$ and describe the transformation of the graph of $y=T(m)$ that gives the graph of $y=g(h)$. [3] (b) Find the time in hours, to 3 significant figures, at which the liquid reaches $50^\circ$C, using $g$. [2] (c) Write down the time found in part (b) in minutes, to 3 significant figures, and verify it using $T$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(h)=20+60e^{-3h}$ [A1]; horizontal stretch [M1] with scale factor $\dfrac{1}{60}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $20+60e^{-3h}=50$ [M1]; $h=0.231$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.231\times60=13.9$ minutes [A1]; $T(13.9)=20+60e^{-0.693}=50$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Replacing $m$ by $60h$ compresses the horizontal scale by a factor of $60$.

subtopic: A transformed exponential and its inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=3e^{(x-1)/2}-4$. (a) Find the range of $f$ and the equation of its horizontal asymptote. [2] (b) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [4] (c) The graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ meet where $f(x)=x$. Find the coordinates of the two points of intersection, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Range $f(x)\gt-4$ [A1]; asymptote $y=-4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y+4=3e^{(x-1)/2}$ [M1]; $\ln\dfrac{y+4}{3}=\dfrac{x-1}{2}$ [A1]; $f^{-1}(x)=1+2\ln\!\left(\dfrac{x+4}{3}\right)$ [A1]; domain $x\gt-4$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Solve $3e^{(x-1)/2}-4=x$ [M1]; $x=-3.72$ [A1]; $x=2.57$, with $y=x$ at each point [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Graphs of a function and its inverse are reflections of each other in the line $y=x$, so any intersection on that line satisfies $f(x)=x$.

subtopic: Mirror-image tides
statement: The height in meters of the tide at harbor A, $t$ hours after midnight, is modeled by $h(t)=3+2\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi(t-2)}{6.2}\right)$ for $0\le t\le24$. At a second harbor B the tide happens in the reverse order of time and its height is $h(24-t)$. (a) State the transformation that maps the graph of $y=h(t)$ onto the graph of the height at harbor B, and write down the greatest height at harbor B. [2] (b) Find the times at which the two harbors have the same tide height, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the length of time, in minutes to the nearest minute, during which both harbors have tide height at least $3.5$ m. [4]
markscheme: (a) Reflection in the line $t=12$ [A1]; greatest height $5$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solve $h(t)=h(24-t)$ [M1]; $t=5.80$ [A1]; $t=12.0$ and $t=18.2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $h(t)\ge3.5$ and $h(24-t)\ge3.5$ [M1]; both hold for $11.8\le t\le12.2$ [A1][A1]; duration $=0.403$ hours $=24$ minutes [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Reflecting in the vertical line $t=a$ replaces $t$ by $2a-t$. Here $a=12$.

subtopic: Absolute value of a quadratic: an inequality
statement: Let $g(x)=\left|x^2-6x+5\right|$. (a) Describe how the graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from the graph of $y=x^2-6x+5$, and write down the $x$-intercepts and the $y$-intercept of $y=g(x)$. [3] (b) Find the least value of $x^2-6x+5$ and hence the greatest value of $g(x)$ on the interval $1\le x\le5$. [3] (c) Solve $g(x)\lt3$, giving exact endpoints where possible. [5]
markscheme: (a) Any part below the $x$-axis is reflected in the $x$-axis [A1]; $x$-intercepts: $x=1$ and $x=5$ [A1]; $y$-intercept $=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(x-3)^2-4$ so least value $-4$ at $x=3$ [A1][M1]; greatest value of $g$ on $[1, 5]$ is $4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-3\lt x^2-6x+5\lt3$ [M1]; $x^2-6x+2\lt0$ gives $3-\sqrt7\lt x\lt3+\sqrt7$ [A1][A1]; $x^2-6x+8\gt0$ gives $x\lt2$ or $x\gt4$ [A1]; solution $3-\sqrt7\lt x\lt2$ or $4\lt x\lt3+\sqrt7$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Split $|u|\lt3$ into $-3\lt u\lt3$, then solve each quadratic inequality and combine the results.

subtopic: Transformations of a cubic and its turning points
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x$. This question investigates how transformations of the graph of $f$ move its turning points and change its gradients. (a) Find the coordinates of the turning points of the graph of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature. [4] (b) The graph of $y=g(x)$ has equation $g(x)=2f(x-1)+3$. Write down the transformations from $y=f(x)$ and the coordinates of the turning points of $y=g(x)$. [4] (c) Show that if $p(x)=a\,f(bx+c)+d$, then $p'(x)=ab\,f'(bx+c)$, and find the gradient of $y=g(x)$ at $x=3$. [4] (d) The curve $y=h(x)$ with $h(x)=p\,f(qx+r)+s$ has a local maximum at $(4, 10)$ and a local minimum at $(8, 2)$, where $q\gt0$ and $p\gt0$. Find $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$. [5] (e) For the curve in part (d), find the coordinates of the point of inflection and the gradient there. State the nature of the gradient there compared with the gradients at the turning points. [4] (f) Find the exact $x$-coordinates where the curve of part (d) crosses the line $y=6$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2-3=0$ [M1]; $x=\pm1$ [A1]; $f(-1)=2$, $f(1)=-2$ [A1]; $f''(x)=6x$: $f''(-1)\lt0$ so $(-1, 2)$ is a local maximum and $f''(1)\gt0$ so $(1, -2)$ is a local minimum [A1] [4 marks] (b) Translation $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, vertical stretch with scale factor $2$, translation $\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; local maximum $(0, 7)$ [A1]; local minimum $(2, -1)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Chain rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}f(bx+c)=b\,f'(bx+c)$ [M1]; so $p'(x)=ab\,f'(bx+c)$ [AG]; for $g$: $g'(x)=2f'(x-1)=2\left(3(x-1)^2-3\right)$ [M1]; $g'(3)=2(12-3)=18$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) Maximum maps $(-1, 2)\to(4, 10)$ and minimum maps $(1, -2)\to(8, 2)$ [R1]; $q(4)+r=-1$ and $q(8)+r=1$ so $q=\dfrac12$, $r=-3$ [M1][A1]; $2p+s=10$ and $-2p+s=2$ so $p=2$, $s=6$ [M1][A1] [5 marks] (e) The point of inflection of $f$ is $(0, 0)$, so $\dfrac{x}{2}-3=0$ [M1]; $x=6$, $y=6$, i.e. $(6, 6)$ [A1]; gradient $=pq\,f'(0)=2\times\dfrac12\times(-3)=-3$ [A1]; the gradient is steepest (most negative) there, compared with $0$ at the turning points [R1] [4 marks] (f) $2f\!\left(\dfrac x2-3\right)+6=6$ so $f(u)=0$ with $u=\dfrac x2-3$ [M1]; $u=0$ or $u=\pm\sqrt3$ [A1]; $x=6$ and $x=6\pm2\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A transformation of the graph moves each turning point by the same transformation. The chain rule shows how the gradient is scaled.

subtopic: Domain and range of a logarithm of a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(4-x^2\right)$. (a) Find the largest possible domain of $f$. [2] (b) Find the range of $f$. [2] (c) Find the exact values of $x$ for which $f(x)=0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Need $4-x^2\gt0$ [M1]; $-2\lt x\lt2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0\lt4-x^2\le4$ on the domain [M1]; $f(x)\le\ln4$ (and takes all values below) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4-x^2=1$ [M1]; $x=\pm\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A logarithm needs a positive argument. The argument takes values up to $4$ but never reaches $0$.

subtopic: A function that is its own inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-2}$ for $x\neq2$. (a) Show that $f(f(x))=x$ for all $x\neq2$, and explain what this tells you about $f^{-1}$. [5] (b) Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $f$, and the range of $f$. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f(f(x))=\dfrac{2\left(\frac{2x+1}{x-2}\right)+1}{\frac{2x+1}{x-2}-2}$ [M1]; numerator $=\dfrac{4x+2+x-2}{x-2}=\dfrac{5x}{x-2}$ [A1]; denominator $=\dfrac{2x+1-2x+4}{x-2}=\dfrac{5}{x-2}$ [A1]; $f(f(x))=x$ [AG]; so $f^{-1}=f$ (self-inverse) [R1] [5 marks] (b) Vertical $x=2$ [A1]; horizontal $y=2$ [A1]; range $f(x)\neq2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2x+1=x(x-2)$ [M1]; $x^2-4x-1=0$, $x=2\pm\sqrt5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If $f(f(x))=x$ then applying $f$ twice returns the original input, so $f$ is its own inverse.

subtopic: A rational function with two vertical asymptotes
statement: Let $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x^2-4}$. (a) Write down the equations of all asymptotes of the graph of $g$. [3] (b) Find the $x$-intercepts and the $y$-intercept. [2] (c) Write $g(x)$ in the form $1+\dfrac{k}{x^2-4}$ and hence show that the value $y=1$ is never taken by $g$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Vertical: $x=2$ and $x=-2$ [A1][A1]; horizontal: $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=\pm1$ [A1]; $g(0)=\dfrac{-1}{-4}=\dfrac14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{x^2-4+3}{x^2-4}=1+\dfrac{3}{x^2-4}$ so $k=3$ [A1]; $y=1$ would need $\dfrac{3}{x^2-4}=0$ [M1], which is impossible [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide the numerator by the denominator (or add and subtract $3$ in the numerator) to find the horizontal asymptote.

subtopic: Symmetry about a vertical line
statement: A quadratic function $f$ satisfies $f(0)=f(6)=5$ and its least value is $-4$. (a) Write down the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $f$ and the coordinates of the vertex. [3] (b) Find $f(x)$ in the form $a(x-h)^2+k$. [2] (c) Find the zeros of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Equal values at $x=0$ and $x=6$, so the axis is $x=3$ [M1][A1]; vertex $(3, -4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)=a(x-3)^2-4$ [A1]; $f(0)=9a-4=5$ so $a=1$ and $f(x)=(x-3)^2-4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(x-3)^2=4$ [M1]; $x=1$ and $x=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A parabola takes equal values at points equidistant from its axis, so the axis is midway between $x=0$ and $x=6$.

subtopic: Evaluating a periodic function
statement: A function $f$ is defined for $x\ge0$ by $f(x)=x^2$ for $0\le x\lt4$, and $f(x+4)=f(x)$ for all $x\ge0$. (a) Find $f(23)$. [2] (b) State the period of $f$ and the range of $f$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)=4$ for $8\le x\lt12$. [2]
tips: Subtract multiples of the period to move the input into the interval where the function is defined.

subtopic: Sum of two absolute values
statement: Let $f(x)=|x-1|+|x+2|$. (a) Write $f(x)$ without modulus signs on each of the three intervals $x\lt-2$, $-2\le x\le1$ and $x\gt1$. [3] (b) State the range of $f$. [1] (c) Solve $f(x)=7$. [2] (d) Explain why $f$ has no inverse function on the domain $\mathbb R$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x\lt-2$: $f(x)=-2x-1$ [A1]; $-2\le x\le1$: $f(x)=3$ [A1]; $x\gt1$: $f(x)=2x+1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)\ge3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $-2x-1=7\Rightarrow x=-4$ [A1]; $2x+1=7\Rightarrow x=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $f$ is not one-to-one, e.g. $f(-4)=f(3)=7$, so it fails the horizontal line test [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Treat each modulus separately: the sign of the expression inside changes at $x=1$ and at $x=-2$.

subtopic: Inverse existence from the derivative
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3+x$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $f$ is an increasing function, and explain why $f$ has an inverse function. [3] (b) Find $f^{-1}(10)$ and $f^{-1}(-2)$. [3] (c) State the domain and the range of $f^{-1}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2+1$ [A1]; $f'(x)\gt0$ for all $x$ so $f$ is increasing [R1]; a strictly increasing function is one-to-one, so it has an inverse [R1] [3 marks] (b) $f(2)=8+2=10$ so $f^{-1}(10)=2$ [M1][A1]; $f(-1)=-1-1=-2$ so $f^{-1}(-2)=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Domain $\mathbb R$, range $\mathbb R$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A cubic with a positive derivative everywhere never turns round, so each output value is produced exactly once.

subtopic: Where an exponential and a quadratic cross
statement: Let $f(x)=2^x$ and $g(x)=x^2$. (a) Find all values of $x$ for which $f(x)=g(x)$, to 3 significant figures where necessary. [3] (b) Hence solve $2^x\gt x^2$. [3] (c) Explain, without calculation, why $2^x\gt x^2$ for all sufficiently large $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Intersections of the graphs on the calculator [M1]; $x=-0.767$ [A1]; $x=2$ and $x=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Compare the two graphs between the intersection points [M1]; $2^x\gt x^2$ for $-0.767\lt x\lt2$ [A1]; and for $x\gt4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) An exponential function eventually grows faster than any polynomial [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Check a test value in each interval (for example $x=3$) to see which function is larger.

subtopic: Cubic model through four points
statement: A cubic function $f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ passes through the points $(0, 5)$, $(1, 6)$, $(2, 3)$ and $(3, 14)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ by solving a system of equations. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum of the graph, to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Find the number of solutions of $f(x)=4$ and explain how you know. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d=5$ [A1]; $a+b+c=1$, $8a+4b+2c=-2$, $27a+9b+3c=9$ [M1][A1]; $a=3, \ b=-11, \ c=9$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $f'(x)=9x^2-22x+9=0$ [M1]; $x=0.519$ and $x=1.92$ [A1]; local maximum $(0.519, 7.13)$ [A1]; local minimum $(1.92, 2.96)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $f(x)=4$ lies between the local minimum $2.96$ and local maximum $7.13$, so the horizontal line $y=4$ cuts the cubic three times [R1]; three solutions [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Four points give four equations in the four unknown coefficients. Solve them with a matrix or the polynomial regression feature.

subtopic: Evaluating an inverse function numerically
statement: Let $h(x)=x^3+2x-5$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $h$ is one-to-one. [2] (b) Find $h^{-1}(10)$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find $h^{-1}(-8)$ and verify your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $h'(x)=3x^2+2\gt0$ [A1]; so $h$ is strictly increasing and one-to-one [R1] [2 marks] (b) Solve $x^3+2x-5=10$ [M1]; $x=2.20$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $x^3+2x-5=-8$: $x=-1$ [A1]; check $(-1)^3-2-5=-8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To evaluate an inverse function at a number $b$, solve $h(x)=b$.

subtopic: Parallel resistors: a rational model
statement: Two resistors of $20$ ohms and $x$ ohms are connected in parallel. The combined resistance is $R(x)=\dfrac{20x}{20+x}$ ohms, for $x\gt0$. (a) Find $R(30)$ and the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $R$. Interpret the asymptote. [3] (b) State the range of $R$ for $x\gt0$ and show that $R$ is one-to-one. [3] (c) Find an expression for $R^{-1}(y)$, the resistance $x$ needed for a combined resistance $y$, and state its domain. [3] (d) Find the value of $x$ that gives a combined resistance of $15$ ohms. [1]
markscheme: (a) $R(30)=\dfrac{600}{50}=12$ ohms [A1]; $R=\dfrac{20}{\frac{20}{x}+1}\to20$ as $x\to\infty$, asymptote $R=20$ [A1]; however large $x$ is, the combined resistance stays below $20$ ohms, the value of the first resistor alone [R1] [3 marks] (b) Range $0\lt R\lt20$ [A1]; $R=20-\dfrac{400}{20+x}$ [M1]; this is strictly increasing [R1] [3 marks] (c) $y(20+x)=20x$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{20y}{20-y}$ [A1]; domain $0\lt y\lt20$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $R^{-1}(15)=\dfrac{300}{5}=60$ ohms [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Rewrite $R$ as $20-\dfrac{400}{20+x}$ to see its behavior and to find the inverse.

subtopic: Number of solutions for $x+2\sin x$
statement: Let $f(x)=x+2\sin x$ for $0\le x\le12$, where $x$ is in radians. (a) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum of the graph of $f$ for $0\lt x\lt6$, to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Solve $f(x)=3$ for $0\le x\le12$, giving all solutions to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the range of values of $k$ for which $f(x)=k$ has exactly three solutions with $0\lt x\lt6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=1+2\cos x=0$ [M1]; $\cos x=-\dfrac12$ so $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [A1]; local maximum $(2.09, 3.83)$ [A1]; local minimum $(4.19, 2.46)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Intersect with $y=3$ [M1]; $x=1.16$ [A1]; $x=3.28$ and $x=4.95$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $k$ must lie strictly between the local minimum and the local maximum [R1]; $2.46\lt k\lt3.83$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The derivative $1+2\cos x$ changes sign, so $f$ is not monotonic. The turning values separate the cases for the number of solutions.

subtopic: Minimum of a reciprocal sum
statement: Let $f(x)=x+\dfrac{9}{x}$ for $x\gt0$. (a) Find the coordinates of the minimum point of the graph of $f$. [3] (b) State the range of $f$ and the number of solutions of $f(x)=k$ for $k\gt6$, $k=6$ and $k\lt6$. [3] (c) Show that $f(x)=10$ has solutions $x=1$ and $x=9$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Calculator minimum, or $f'(x)=1-\dfrac{9}{x^2}=0$ [M1]; $x=3$ [A1]; $(3, 6)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Range $f(x)\ge6$ [A1]; $k\gt6$: two solutions [A1]; $k=6$: one solution; $k\lt6$: none [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x^2-10x+9=0$ [M1]; $(x-1)(x-9)=0$ [AG] [2 marks]
tips: Multiply $x+\dfrac9x=10$ by $x$ to obtain a quadratic equation.

subtopic: An equation in tangent squared
statement: Solve $\tan^2x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, giving exact answers in radians. (a) Find all the solutions. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\tan x=\sqrt3$ or $\tan x=-\sqrt3$ [M1]; $\tan x=\sqrt3$: $x=\dfrac\pi3, \ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [A1]; $\tan x=-\sqrt3$: $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: Take square roots of both sides and remember both signs. Tangent has period $\pi$.

subtopic: The graph of $y=\tan 2x$
statement: Consider the function $f(x)=\tan2x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. (a) Find the period of $f$ and write down the equations of its vertical asymptotes in the interval $0\le x\le\pi$. [3] (b) Solve $f(x)=1$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, giving exact answers. [3] (c) Write down the values of $x$ in the interval for which $f(x)=0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Period $=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1]; $2x=\dfrac\pi2+n\pi$ [M1]; asymptotes $x=\dfrac\pi4$ and $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2x=\dfrac\pi4+n\pi$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac\pi8$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{8}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2x=n\pi$ [M1]; $x=0, \ \dfrac\pi2, \ \pi$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Replacing $x$ by $2x$ halves the period of the tangent function.

subtopic: Triangle with an obtuse angle: exact area and third side
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$ cm, $AC=5$ cm and angle $BAC=120^\circ$. (a) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (b) Find the exact length of $BC$. [3] (c) Find the exact perpendicular distance from $A$ to $BC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12\times8\times5\times\sin120^\circ$ [M1] $=20\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=10\sqrt3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $BC^2=8^2+5^2-2\times8\times5\cos120^\circ$ [M1]; $=64+25+40$ [A1]; $BC=\sqrt{129}$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area $=\dfrac12\times\sqrt{129}\times h=10\sqrt3$ [M1]; $h=\dfrac{20\sqrt3}{\sqrt{129}}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\cos120^\circ=-\frac12$ and $\sin120^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

subtopic: A point on the unit circle
statement: The point $P\left(-\dfrac{5}{13}, -\dfrac{12}{13}\right)$ lies on the unit circle. The angle $\theta$, with $0\le\theta\lt2\pi$, is measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis to $OP$. (a) Write down $\cos\theta$, $\sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta$, and state which quadrant $P$ is in. [3] (b) Express $\theta$ in terms of $\pi$ and an inverse tangent. [2] (c) Find the exact values of $\sin(\theta+\pi)$ and $\cos(\pi-\theta)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{5}{13}$, $\sin\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1]; $\tan\theta=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1]; third quadrant [A1] [3 marks] (b) The reference angle is $\arctan\dfrac{12}{5}$ [M1]; $\theta=\pi+\arctan\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin(\theta+\pi)=-\sin\theta$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1]; $\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: On the unit circle the coordinates of $P$ are $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. Adding $\pi$ to the angle reflects the point through the origin.

subtopic: Angular speed and linear speed
statement: A bicycle wheel of radius $0.3$ m rotates at a constant rate of $2$ complete revolutions per second. (a) Find the angular speed of the wheel in radians per second. [1] (b) Find the exact speed of a point on the outer rim, in m s$^{-1}$, and the exact distance traveled by that point in $3$ seconds. [3] (c) A point on the rim starts at the lowest position. Its height above the ground, in meters, at time $t$ seconds is $h(t)=0.3-0.3\cos(4\pi t)$. Find the exact times in $0\le t\le1$ at which $h(t)=0.45$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2\times2\pi=4\pi$ rad s$^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Speed $=r\omega=0.3\times4\pi$ [M1] $=1.2\pi$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1]; distance $=3\times1.2\pi=3.6\pi$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos(4\pi t)=-\dfrac12$ [M1]; $4\pi t=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ (and the next revolution) [A1]; $t=\dfrac16, \ \dfrac13, \ \dfrac23, \ \dfrac56$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Speed $=$ radius $\times$ angular speed when the angle is measured in radians.

subtopic: Illuminated fraction of the Moon
statement: The fraction $I$ of the Moon's visible face that is lit, $t$ days after a new moon, is modeled by $I(t)=0.5-0.5\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{29.5}\right)$, with the angle in radians and $0\le t\le29.5$. (a) Find the period of the model and the greatest and least values of $I$. [3] (b) Find the fraction lit at $t=5$ days, as a percentage to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the times between which more than $90\%$ of the face is lit, and the number of days this lasts, to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) Period $=29.5$ days [A1]; greatest $I=1$ (full moon) [A1]; least $I=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $I(5)=0.5-0.5\cos(1.065)$ [M1] $=25.8\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $0.5-0.5\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{29.5}\right)=0.9$ [M1]; $t=11.7$ [A1]; $t=17.8$ [A1]; duration $=6.04$ days [A1] [4 marks]
tips: More than $90\%$ lit means $\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{29.5}\right)\lt-0.8$. Use the intersection feature with $y=0.9$.

subtopic: Two possible triangles from the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $BAC=30^\circ$, $BC=5$ cm and $AC=8$ cm. (a) Use the sine rule to find the two possible sizes of angle $ABC$. [3] (b) For each possible triangle, find the length of $AB$, to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Find the area of the smaller of the two triangles, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin B}{8}=\dfrac{\sin30^\circ}{5}$ [M1]; $\sin B=0.8$ [A1]; $B=53.1^\circ$ or $B=127^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $B=53.1^\circ$: $C=96.9^\circ$, $AB=\dfrac{5\sin96.87^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=9.93$ cm [M1][A1]; $B=126.9^\circ$: $C=23.1^\circ$, $AB=\dfrac{5\sin23.13^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=3.93$ cm [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\times8\times3.93\times\sin30^\circ$ [M1] $=7.86\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The sine rule gives $\sin B$, which has two solutions between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$: an acute angle and its supplement.

subtopic: A partly filled circular pipe
statement: A horizontal pipe has a circular cross-section of radius $0.5$ m. When water in the pipe has depth $d$ m at the lowest point, the surface of the water subtends an angle $\theta$ radians at the center of the circle. The area of the cross-section occupied by the water is $A=\dfrac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)$ with $r=0.5$. (a) Show that the pipe is half full when $\theta=\pi$. [2] (b) The water occupies $30\%$ of the cross-section area. Find $\theta$, in radians to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the depth $d$ of the water at the lowest point for this value of $\theta$, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=\dfrac12\times0.25\times(\pi-0)$ [M1] $=0.125\pi$, which is half of the pipe's cross-section area $0.25\pi$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac12(0.25)(\theta-\sin\theta)=0.3\times\pi\times0.25$ [M1]; solve $\theta-\sin\theta=2.356$ [A1]; $\theta=2.49$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Depth $=r-r\cos\dfrac\theta2$ [M1]; $=0.5-0.5\cos(1.2454)$ [A1]; $=0.340$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The surface chord makes an isosceles triangle with the two radii. The distance from the center to the water surface is $r\cos\frac\theta2$.

subtopic: Launch angle for a given range
statement: A ball is launched from level ground with speed $20$ m s$^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, where $0^\circ\lt\theta\lt90^\circ$. Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance it travels before landing is $R=\dfrac{v^2}{g}\sin2\theta$ with $v=20$ and $g=9.8$. (a) Find the greatest possible range and the angle at which it occurs, to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) The ball must land $30$ m away. Find the two possible launch angles, to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Show that the two angles in part (b) sum to $90^\circ$, and explain why this happens using the graph of $\sin2\theta$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Greatest value of $\sin2\theta$ is $1$ [M1]; $R_{\max}=\dfrac{400}{9.8}=40.8$ m [A1]; at $\theta=45^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sin2\theta=\dfrac{30\times9.8}{400}=0.735$ [M1]; $2\theta=47.3^\circ$ or $132.7^\circ$ [A1]; $\theta=23.7^\circ$ [A1]; $\theta=66.3^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $23.65^\circ+66.35^\circ=90^\circ$ [A1]; the graph of $\sin2\theta$ is symmetric about $\theta=45^\circ$, so angles equally far either side give the same range [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Isolate $\sin 2\theta$, then remember that sine takes each value in $(0, 1)$ twice between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.

subtopic: Visibility from a satellite
statement: A satellite is at height $h=35786$ km above the surface of the Earth, which is modeled as a sphere of radius $R=6371$ km with center $O$. From the satellite, the visible part of the surface is bounded by the circle of points where the line of sight just touches the Earth. Let $\theta$ be the angle at $O$ between the line to the satellite and the line to a point $T$ on this boundary circle. (a) Explain why $\cos\theta=\dfrac{R}{R+h}$ and find $\theta$, in degrees to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the distance along the surface from the point directly below the satellite to the boundary of the visible region, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) The area of the visible cap is $2\pi R^2(1-\cos\theta)$. Find the percentage of the Earth's surface area, $4\pi R^2$, that is visible, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Triangle $OTS$ has a right angle at $T$ (the tangent is perpendicular to the radius) [R1]; $\cos\theta=\dfrac{OT}{OS}=\dfrac{R}{R+h}$ [AG]; $\cos\theta=\dfrac{6371}{42157}$ [M1]; $\theta=81.3^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Arc $=R\theta=6371\times1.419$ [M1] $=9040$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) Fraction $=\dfrac{2\pi R^2(1-\cos\theta)}{4\pi R^2}=\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{2}$ [M1]; $\cos\theta=0.1511$ [A1]; $42.4\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The line of sight to the boundary is tangent to the sphere, so it is perpendicular to the radius at that point.

subtopic: Belt around two pulleys
statement: A belt goes around two circular pulleys of radii $10$ cm and $4$ cm whose centers are $30$ cm apart, in the open arrangement (the belt does not cross itself), so that the belt touches each pulley along an arc and the two straight parts of the belt are common tangents. Let $\alpha$ be the angle between each straight part of the belt and the line joining the centers. (a) Show that $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{10-4}{30}$ and find $\alpha$ in radians to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the length of each straight part of the belt, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) The belt wraps around the larger pulley through an angle $\pi+2\alpha$ and around the smaller pulley through $\pi-2\alpha$. Find the total length of the belt, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Draw a line from the center of the smaller pulley parallel to a straight part of the belt: right triangle with hypotenuse $30$ and opposite side $10-4=6$ [M1]; $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{6}{30}=0.2$ [AG]; $\alpha=0.201$ rad [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt{30^2-6^2}$ [M1] $=29.4$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Arc on large pulley $=10(\pi+2\alpha)=35.4$ [M1]; arc on small pulley $=4(\pi-2\alpha)=11.0$ [A1]; total $=2\times29.39+35.4+11.0=105$ cm [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The radii to the points of contact are both perpendicular to the straight part of the belt, so they are parallel.

subtopic: Does the Voronoi vertex lie inside the triangle?
statement: Three sites are $X(0, 0)$, $Y(6, 0)$ and $Z(1, 2)$. (a) Find $XY^2$, $XZ^2$ and $YZ^2$, and use them to decide whether angle $XZY$ is acute, right or obtuse. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex of the three sites. [4] (c) State, with a reason, whether the Voronoi vertex lies inside or outside triangle $XYZ$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $XY^2=36$, $XZ^2=5$, $YZ^2=25+4=29$ [A1]; compare $36$ with $5+29=34$ [M1]; $XY^2\gt XZ^2+YZ^2$ so the angle at $Z$ is obtuse [A1] [3 marks] (b) The bisector of $XY$ is $x=3$ [A1]; equidistance from $X$ and $Z$: $9+y^2=4+(y-2)^2$ [M1]; $9+y^2=y^2-4y+8$ so $y=-\dfrac14$ [A1]; vertex $\left(3, -\dfrac14\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Outside, because it lies below the $x$-axis while the triangle lies above it (the triangle has an obtuse angle) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The circumcenter of a triangle lies inside it for an acute triangle, on the longest side for a right triangle and outside it for an obtuse triangle.

subtopic: Moving and scaling the sites
statement: Three sites are $A(1, 0)$, $B(5, 0)$ and $C(3, 4)$. (a) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex $V$ of the three sites and the distance from $V$ to each site. [4] (b) Every site is now mapped by $(x, y)\to(2x+3, \ 2y-1)$ (an enlargement with scale factor $2$ followed by a translation). Write down the new sites, the new Voronoi vertex and its distance to each new site, without recalculating the bisectors. [4]
markscheme: (a) Bisector of $AB$: $x=3$ [A1]; $(3-1)^2+y^2=(y-4)^2$ [M1]; $4+y^2=y^2-8y+16$, $y=\dfrac32$ [A1]; $V\left(3, \dfrac32\right)$ with distance $\sqrt{4+\dfrac94}=\dfrac52$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) New sites: $(5, -1)$, $(13, -1)$, $(9, 7)$ [A1]; every Voronoi boundary and vertex is mapped in the same way so $V'=(2\times3+3, \ 2\times\dfrac32-1)=(9, 2)$ [A1][M1]; distance doubles to $5$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: An enlargement multiplies all distances by the scale factor and a translation does not change them. The Voronoi vertex is the image of the old vertex.

subtopic: The cell of a site in a triangular arrangement
statement: A site $O$ is at the origin and three other sites are at $P(4, 0)$, $Q(-2, 2\sqrt3)$ and $R(-2, -2\sqrt3)$. (a) Show that $OP=OQ=OR=4$ and find the equations of the three bisectors of $OP$, $OQ$ and $OR$. [4] (b) The cell of $O$ is the triangle bounded by these three lines. Find the coordinates of its vertices. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the cell of $O$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $OQ=\sqrt{4+12}=4$ and $OR=4$ [A1]; bisector of $OP$: $x=2$ [A1]; bisector of $OQ$: $x-\sqrt3y+4=0$ [M1]; bisector of $OR$: $x+\sqrt3y+4=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $x=2$ with the second line: $y=2\sqrt3$, vertex $(2, 2\sqrt3)$ [A1]; $x=2$ with the third line: $(2, -2\sqrt3)$ [A1]; the second and third lines: $(-4, 0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Base $=4\sqrt3$, height $=6$ [A1][A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times4\sqrt3\times6=12\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The bisector of $O$ and a point $(a, b)$ is $ax+by=\dfrac{a^2+b^2}{2}$. The cell is the set of points on the same side of each bisector as $O$.

subtopic: Equation of a Voronoi boundary in general form
statement: Two sites are $A(a, b)$ and $B(c, d)$. (a) By equating the squared distances from a general point $(x, y)$ to $A$ and to $B$, show that the boundary between their cells has equation $2(c-a)x+2(d-b)y=c^2+d^2-a^2-b^2$. [3] (b) Use the formula for $A(-1, 2)$ and $B(5, -2)$ to find the equation of the boundary in the form $px+qy=r$, and verify that the midpoint of $AB$ lies on it. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=(x-c)^2+(y-d)^2$ [M1]; expand: $-2ax+a^2-2by+b^2=-2cx+c^2-2dy+d^2$ [A1]; rearrange to give the result [AG] [3 marks] (b) $12x-8y=25+4-1-4=24$ [M1]; $3x-2y=6$ [A1]; midpoint $(2, 0)$: $6-0=6$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Squares of $x$ and $y$ cancel when you equate the two squared distances, leaving a linear equation.

subtopic: Walking along a line through three cells
statement: Three sites are $A(0, 0)$, $B(6, 0)$ and $C(3, 5)$. A person walks along the vertical line $x=3$, from $(3, 0)$ upward. (a) Show that the Voronoi vertex of the three sites is $\left(3, \dfrac85\right)$. [3] (b) Show that the point $(3, 1)$ is equally close to $A$ and $B$ and closer to them than to $C$, and find the site that is nearest to the point $(3, 3)$. [3] (c) Find the exact distance from the vertex to each site. [2]
markscheme: (a) Every point on $x=3$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$ [R1]; equidistance from $A$ and $C$ for $(3, y)$: $9+y^2=(5-y)^2$ [M1]; $y=\dfrac{16}{10}=\dfrac85$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $(3, 1)$: distances $\sqrt{9+1}=\sqrt{10}$ to both $A$ and $B$ [A1]; distance to $C$ is $4=\sqrt{16}\gt\sqrt{10}$ [A1]; $(3, 3)$: distance to $C$ is $2$ while to $A$ and $B$ it is $\sqrt{18}$, so $C$ is nearest [A1] [3 marks] (c) To $C$: $5-\dfrac85=\dfrac{17}{5}$ [M1]; and to $A$: $\sqrt{9+\dfrac{64}{25}}=\dfrac{17}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The vertex is equidistant from all three sites. Points on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ are equally far from $A$ and $B$.

subtopic: Bounded and unbounded cells for six sites
statement: Six wells are at the sites $A(1, 1)$, $B(9, 0)$, $C(11, 6)$, $D(5, 10)$, $E(0, 7)$ and $F(5, 5)$, with coordinates in kilometers. Consider the Voronoi diagram of the six sites. (a) The sites $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ form a convex pentagon with $F$ inside it. State which cells are unbounded and which cell is bounded, with a reason. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertices of the cell of $F$, to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Find the area of the cell of $F$, to 3 significant figures, using the unrounded vertices. [3] (d) Find the length of the boundary shared by the cells of $D$ and $F$, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) The cells of $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ are unbounded because those sites are on the boundary of the convex hull [R1]; the cell of $F$ is bounded because $F$ is surrounded by the other sites [A1] [2 marks] (b) Vertices are circumcenters of $F$ with consecutive neighbors, found by solving two bisector equations each [M1]: $(A,B,F)$: $(5.06, 0.944)$ [A1]; $(B,C,F)$: $(8.32, 3.56)$, $(C,D,F)$: $(7.67, 7.50)$ [A1]; $(D,E,F)$: $(3.10, 7.50)$, $(E,A,F)$: $(1.79, 4.21)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Shoelace formula on the five vertices in order [M1][A1]; area $=29.8\ \text{km}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Distance between $(7.667, 7.5)$ and $(3.1, 7.5)$ [M1] $=4.57$ km [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A cell is unbounded exactly when its site lies on the boundary of the convex hull of all the sites.

subtopic: Four nearly cocircular sites
statement: Four sites are $A(0, 0)$, $B(8, 0)$, $C(8, 6)$ and $D(0, d)$ where $d\gt0$ is a constant. (a) For $d=6$, show that the four sites are the same distance from the point $(4, 3)$, and state what this means for the Voronoi diagram at that point. [3] (b) Now let $d=7$. Show that the circle through $A$, $B$, $C$ does not contain $D$, and find the Voronoi vertex of $A$, $C$ and $D$ to 4 significant figures. [4] (c) For $d=7$ there are two Voronoi vertices, one for $A$, $B$, $C$ and one for $A$, $C$, $D$. Find which two cells share the boundary segment between these vertices and the length of that segment, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Distances from $(4, 3)$: to $A$, $B$, $C$, $D=(0, 6)$: each is $\sqrt{16+9}=5$ [M1][A1]; four cells meet at a single vertex [R1] [3 marks] (b) Circle through $A$, $B$, $C$ has center $(4, 3)$ and radius $5$; $D(0, 7)$ is at distance $\sqrt{32}=5.66\gt5$ [M1][A1]; for $A$, $C$, $D$: bisector of $AD$ is $y=3.5$ and of $AC$ is $8x+6y=50$ [M1]; vertex $(3.625, 3.5)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The vertices are $(4, 3)$ and $(3.625, 3.5)$ [A1]; both are on the bisector of $A$ and $C$, so cells $A$ and $C$ share the segment [A1]; length $=\sqrt{0.375^2+0.5^2}=0.625$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For four points, which pair of cells shares an edge depends on whether the fourth site lies inside the circle through the other three.

subtopic: Central cell surrounded by a ring of sites
statement: A central site $O$ is at the origin and $n$ other sites are equally spaced on a circle of radius $8$ km centered at $O$, with $n\ge3$. (a) Show that the boundary between the cell of $O$ and the cell of a ring site is at distance $4$ km from $O$. [2] (b) Explain why the cell of $O$ is a regular $n$-sided polygon, and show that its area is $16n\tan\dfrac\pi n$ square kilometers. [4] (c) Find the area of the cell of $O$ and the distance from $O$ to each vertex of the cell, for $n=5$, $n=6$ and $n=8$, to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) As $n$ becomes very large, the cell approaches a circle of radius $4$ km. Find the area of this circle and compare it with your answer for $n=8$. [2]
markscheme: (a) The boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from $O$ to the ring site, which has length $8$ [M1]; so it is at distance $\dfrac82=4$ from $O$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) By symmetry the $n$ boundaries are at equal distance $4$ from $O$ and equally spaced in direction, so the cell is a regular $n$-gon with inradius $4$ [R1]; it splits into $2n$ right triangles with angle $\dfrac\pi n$ at $O$, adjacent side $4$, and opposite side $4\tan\dfrac\pi n$ [M1]; area $=2n\times\dfrac12\times4\times4\tan\dfrac\pi n$ [A1]; $=16n\tan\dfrac\pi n$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $n=5$: $58.1\ \text{km}^2$ and $4.94$ km [A1]; $n=6$: $55.4\ \text{km}^2$ and $4.62$ km [A1]; $n=8$: $53.0\ \text{km}^2$ and $4.33$ km [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\pi\times16=50.3\ \text{km}^2$ [A1]; the polygon area decreases towards this value but is still $2.75\ \text{km}^2$ larger when $n=8$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The distance from $O$ to a vertex is $\dfrac{4}{\cos(\pi/n)}$. Compare the values as $n$ grows.

subtopic: Pipeline cost through three service areas
statement: Three pumping stations are at $A(2, 2)$, $B(10, 3)$ and $C(6, 9)$ (kilometers). A straight pipeline runs along the line $y=6$ from the west edge $x=0$ to the east edge $x=12$ of a region. Each part of the pipeline is maintained by the station whose Voronoi cell contains it. The maintenance costs are $5$, $6$ and $8$ thousand dollars per kilometer for the parts maintained by $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively.
