statement: The matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ is given. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{PDP}^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{D}$ diagonal, and hence find $\mathbf{A}^{3}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=\lambda^{2} - 6 \lambda + 5=0$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=5$ and $\lambda=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda=5$: $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=1$: $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{A}^{3}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 32 & 31 \\ 93 & 94 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: An eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies $(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$. Powers are $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{PD}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.

subtopic: Diagonalizing a matrix with a negative eigenvalue
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is given. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{PDP}^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{D}$ diagonal, and hence find $\mathbf{A}^{3}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=\lambda^{2} - 3 \lambda - 4=0$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=4$ and $\lambda=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda=4$: $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=-1$: $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{A}^{3}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 25 & 26 \\ 39 & 38 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: An eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies $(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$. Powers are $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{PD}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain by hand
statement: A machine is either working or broken at the start of each day. The transition matrix $\mathbf{T}$ (columns sum to $1$; state order: working, broken) is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{9}{10} & \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{10} & \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$, and the state vector satisfies $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$. On day $0$ the machine is working with probability $0.4$, so $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{3}{5} \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$. [3] (b) Find $\mathbf{T}^2$ and state the probability that the system is in state broken two steps after being in state working. [3] (c) Find the steady state vector $\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ and the entries summing to $1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{s}_1=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{33}{50} \\ \dfrac{17}{50} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{s}_2=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{191}{250} \\ \dfrac{59}{250} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}^2=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{43}{50} & \dfrac{7}{10} \\ \dfrac{7}{50} & \dfrac{3}{10} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; Entry in row 2, column 1 $=\dfrac{7}{50}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} a \\ 1-a \end{pmatrix}$: $\dfrac{9}{10}a+\dfrac{1}{2}(1-a)=a$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{5}{6} \\ \dfrac{1}{6} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each column of $\mathbf{T}$ sums to $1$ and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$. The steady state is the eigenvector for eigenvalue $1$, scaled to sum to $1$.

subtopic: Steady state of a two-state transition matrix
statement: Each year a customer uses either brand $X$ or brand $Y$. With state order $(X, Y)$, the transition matrix (columns sum to $1$) is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{7}{10} & \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{3}{10} & \dfrac{3}{5} \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$. In year $0$ the market is split $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$. [3] (b) Find $\mathbf{T}^2$ and state the probability that the system is in state brand Y two steps after being in state brand X. [3] (c) Find the steady state vector $\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ and the entries summing to $1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{s}_1=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{11}{20} \\ \dfrac{9}{20} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{s}_2=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{113}{200} \\ \dfrac{87}{200} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}^2=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{61}{100} & \dfrac{13}{25} \\ \dfrac{39}{100} & \dfrac{12}{25} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; Entry in row 2, column 1 $=\dfrac{39}{100}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} a \\ 1-a \end{pmatrix}$: $\dfrac{7}{10}a+\dfrac{2}{5}(1-a)=a$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{4}{7} \\ \dfrac{3}{7} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each column of $\mathbf{T}$ sums to $1$ and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$. The steady state is the eigenvector for eigenvalue $1$, scaled to sum to $1$.

subtopic: Solving a pricing system using the inverse matrix
statement: A fruit stall sells small boxes costing $\$x$ each and large boxes costing $\$y$ each. Three small boxes and two large boxes cost $\$17$ in total. Five small boxes and four large boxes cost $\$31$ in total. (a) Write the information as a matrix equation $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{b}$, and find $\det\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$. [4] (b) Hence find the cost of one small box and of one large box. [3] (c) A customer buys 2 small boxes and 3 large boxes. Find the total cost. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 17 \\ 31 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\det\mathbf{A}=2$ [A1]; $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=3$, $y=4$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $2\times3+3\times4$ [M1]; $18$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A system $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has solution $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ when $\det\mathbf{A}\ne0$.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for travel mode
statement: Commuters choose between car, bus and bike each month. With state order (car, bus, bike), the transition matrix $\mathbf{T}$ (columns sum to $1$) is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$. Initially $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0.3 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the state vector $\mathbf{s}_{4}$ after 4 steps, to $3$ decimal places. [3] (b) Find the steady state vector, to $3$ decimal places. [3] (c) In the long run, a total of 12000 commuters is split between the three states. Find the expected number in each state, to the nearest whole number. [2] (d) Find the smallest number of steps $n$ for which every entry of $\mathbf{s}_n$ is within $0.005$ of the steady state. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{s}_{4}=\mathbf{T}^{4}\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0.360 \\ 0.373 \\ 0.267 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $(\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{0}$ with the entries summing to $1$ (or eigenvector of eigenvalue $1$ on the GDC) [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0.345 \\ 0.379 \\ 0.276 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) 12000 times the steady state [M1]; car: 4138, bus: 4552, bike: 3310 [A1] [2 marks] (d) Compute $\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$ on the GDC for $n=1, 2, \ldots$ [M1]; $n=6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Columns of $\mathbf{T}$ sum to $1$. $\mathbf{s}_n=\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$. For a regular chain, $\mathbf{s}_n$ approaches the steady state whatever $\mathbf{s}_0$ is.

subtopic: Brand switching among three supermarkets
statement: A town has three supermarkets $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$. Each week customers move between them with transition matrix (columns sum to $1$) $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$, and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$. In week $0$ the shares are $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 0.2 \\ 0.5 \\ 0.3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the state vector $\mathbf{s}_{5}$ after 5 steps, to $3$ decimal places. [3] (b) Find the steady state vector, to $3$ decimal places. [3] (c) In the long run, a total of 9500 customers is split between the three states. Find the expected number in each state, to the nearest whole number. [2] (d) Find the smallest number of steps $n$ for which every entry of $\mathbf{s}_n$ is within $0.005$ of the steady state. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{s}_{5}=\mathbf{T}^{5}\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0.391 \\ 0.335 \\ 0.274 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $(\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{0}$ with the entries summing to $1$ (or eigenvector of eigenvalue $1$ on the GDC) [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0.421 \\ 0.316 \\ 0.263 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) 9500 times the steady state [M1]; S1: 4000, S2: 3000, S3: 2500 [A1] [2 marks] (d) Compute $\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$ on the GDC for $n=1, 2, \ldots$ [M1]; $n=10$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Columns of $\mathbf{T}$ sum to $1$. $\mathbf{s}_n=\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$. For a regular chain, $\mathbf{s}_n$ approaches the steady state whatever $\mathbf{s}_0$ is.

subtopic: Two-stage population model with a dominant eigenvalue
statement: A population of an animal has juveniles and adults. Each year each adult produces on average $1.6$ juveniles, $55\%$ of juveniles become adults and $80\%$ of adults survive. With state order (juveniles, adults), the population vector satisfies $\mathbf{p}_{n+1}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{p}_n$ where $\mathbf{L}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1.6 \\ 0.55 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{p}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 200 \\ 300 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the population vector after 6 years, giving each entry to the nearest whole number. [3] (b) Find the dominant eigenvalue of $\mathbf{L}$ and an eigenvector, and interpret the eigenvalue as a long-term yearly growth factor. Give the eigenvector scaled to sum to $1$, to $3$ decimal places. [4] (c) Use the matrix power on your GDC to find the first year in which the total population is at least double its initial total. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{p}_{6}=\mathbf{L}^{6}\mathbf{p}_0$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 2420 \\ 2155 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda^2-0.8\lambda-0.88=0$ [M1]; $\lambda=1.420$ [A1]; Eigenvector $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.530 \\ 0.470 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; Each year the population is multiplied by about 1.42, a growth of 42.0\% per year [A1] [4 marks] (c) Compute $\mathbf{L}^n\mathbf{p}_0$ and its total for $n=1, 2, \ldots$ [M1]; $n=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A Leslie matrix has fecundity in the first row and survival rates below. The dominant eigenvalue is the long-term growth factor, and its eigenvector gives the stable age distribution.

subtopic: Age-structured population of fish
statement: A fish stock has young fish and mature fish. Each year each mature fish produces $2.4$ young fish, $35\%$ of young fish become mature and $60\%$ of mature fish survive. With state order (young, mature), $\mathbf{p}_{n+1}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{p}_n$ with $\mathbf{L}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2.4 \\ 0.35 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{p}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 1000 \\ 400 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the population vector after 8 years, giving each entry to the nearest whole number. [3] (b) Find the dominant eigenvalue of $\mathbf{L}$ and an eigenvector, and interpret the eigenvalue as a long-term yearly growth factor. Give the eigenvector scaled to sum to $1$, to $3$ decimal places. [4] (c) Use the matrix power on your GDC to find the first year in which the total population is at least double its initial total. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{p}_{8}=\mathbf{L}^{8}\mathbf{p}_0$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 5506 \\ 2896 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda^2-0.6\lambda-0.84=0$ [M1]; $\lambda=1.264$ [A1]; Eigenvector $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.655 \\ 0.345 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; Each year the population is multiplied by about 1.26, a growth of 26.4\% per year [A1] [4 marks] (c) Compute $\mathbf{L}^n\mathbf{p}_0$ and its total for $n=1, 2, \ldots$ [M1]; $n=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A Leslie matrix has fecundity in the first row and survival rates below. The dominant eigenvalue is the long-term growth factor, and its eigenvector gives the stable age distribution.

subtopic: Three-item pricing system with a 3 by 3 matrix
statement: A bakery sells cakes, pies and buns. Three orders gave the totals below. With $\mathbf{x}$ the vector of unit prices (in dollars) of a cake, a pie and a bun, the orders give $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ (numbers of cakes, pies, buns in each order) and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 16.8 \\ 15.4 \\ 25.35 \end{pmatrix}$ (totals in dollars). Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$ and explain why the system has a unique solution. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the unit price of each item. [4] (c) A new order contains $2$ cakes, $3$ pies and $10$ buns. Find its total cost. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{A}=-5$ [A1]; The determinant is non-zero, so $\mathbf{A}$ is invertible and the solution is unique [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; cake: $\$4.50$, pie: $\$2.80$, bun: $\$1.25$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $2\times4.5+3\times2.8+10\times1.25$ [M1]; $\$29.90$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A $3\times3$ system can be solved with the inverse matrix on a GDC: $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$.

subtopic: Solving a 3 by 3 system for unit costs
statement: A caterer buys fruit, nuts and grain. Three purchases give $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{x}$ is the vector of prices per kilogram (in dollars) of fruit, nuts and grain, $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ (kilograms of fruit, nuts, grain in each purchase) and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 11.8 \\ 11.6 \\ 11.15 \end{pmatrix}$ (totals in dollars). Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$ and explain why the system has a unique solution. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the unit price of each item. [4] (c) A new order contains $4$ kg of fruit, $2$ kg of nuts and $6$ kg of grain. Find its total cost. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{A}=45$ [A1]; The determinant is non-zero, so $\mathbf{A}$ is invertible and the solution is unique [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; fruit: $\$2.40$, nuts: $\$1.85$, grain: $\$0.90$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $4\times2.4+2\times1.85+6\times0.9$ [M1]; $\$18.70$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A $3\times3$ system can be solved with the inverse matrix on a GDC: $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$.

subtopic: Rate of convergence of a two-state chain
statement: A two-state chain has transition matrix (columns sum to $1$) $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{7}{10} & \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{3}{10} & \dfrac{3}{5} \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$, with $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find the steady state vector of $\mathbf{T}$. [2] (b) Show that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $\dfrac{3}{10}$. [1] (c) Given that the first entry of $\mathbf{s}_n$ is $\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\times(\dfrac{3}{10})^n$, find the smallest number of steps $n$ for which this entry is within $0.001$ of its long-run value. [3] (d) Explain why the sign of $\dfrac{3}{10}$ affects how the first entry of $\mathbf{s}_n$ approaches its long-run value. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ and the entries sum to $1$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{4}{7} \\ \dfrac{3}{7} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of $\mathbf{T}$ and one eigenvalue is $1$ (each column sums to $1$) [M1]; $\lambda_2=\dfrac{13}{10}-1=\dfrac{3}{10}$ [AG] [1 mark] (c) $\left|\dfrac{3}{7}\times(\dfrac{3}{10})^n\right|\lt0.001$ [M1]; $n\gt5.034$ (or table of values on the GDC) [A1]; $n=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The eigenvalue is positive, so the terms keep the same sign and the first entry approaches its limit from one side without oscillating [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The distance from the steady state shrinks by the factor $|\lambda_2|$ at each step.

subtopic: Convergence of a chain with a negative second eigenvalue
statement: A two-state system has transition matrix (columns sum to $1$) $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5} \\ \dfrac{4}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5} \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$, with $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find the steady state vector of $\mathbf{T}$. [2] (b) Show that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $- \dfrac{2}{5}$. [1] (c) Given that the first entry of $\mathbf{s}_n$ is $\dfrac{3}{7}+\dfrac{1}{14}\times(- \dfrac{2}{5})^n$, find the smallest number of steps $n$ for which this entry is within $0.001$ of its long-run value. [3] (d) Explain why the sign of $- \dfrac{2}{5}$ affects how the first entry of $\mathbf{s}_n$ approaches its long-run value. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ and the entries sum to $1$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{3}{7} \\ \dfrac{4}{7} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of $\mathbf{T}$ and one eigenvalue is $1$ (each column sums to $1$) [M1]; $\lambda_2=\dfrac{3}{5}-1=- \dfrac{2}{5}$ [AG] [1 mark] (c) $\left|\dfrac{1}{14}\times(- \dfrac{2}{5})^n\right|\lt0.001$ [M1]; $n\gt4.659$ (or table of values on the GDC) [A1]; $n=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The eigenvalue is negative, so the terms alternate in sign and the first entry oscillates above and below its limit as it converges [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The distance from the steady state shrinks by the factor $|\lambda_2|$ at each step.

subtopic: Customer loyalty model with eigenvalues and diagonalization
statement: A subscription service has customers in state $1$ (active) or state $2$ (inactive) each month. With state vector $\mathbf{s}_n=\begin{pmatrix} a_n \\ b_n \end{pmatrix}$ giving the proportions in each state at month $n$, $\mathbf{s}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}_n$ where $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$. At month $0$, $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 0.3 \\ 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$. [3] (b) Show that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $0.7$. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue, with integer entries, and write $\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{PDP}^{-1}$. [4] (d) Hence show that the proportion of active customers at month $n$ is $a_n=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{11}{30}\left(0.7\right)^n$ (the formula holds for $n\ge0$). [4] (e) Find the smallest $n$ for which the proportion of active customers is within $0.001$ of its long-run value. [3] (f) Each active customer gives the service $\$12$ per month and each inactive customer $\$5$ per month. Find the expected total revenue per customer over months $0$ to $11$, in dollars to the nearest cent. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{s}_1=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{41}{100} \\ \dfrac{59}{100} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{s}_2=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{487}{1000} \\ \dfrac{513}{1000} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det(\mathbf{T}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(0.9-\lambda)(0.8-\lambda)-0.02$ [M1]; $=\lambda^2-1.7\lambda+0.7=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-0.7)$ [A1]; Eigenvalues $1$ and $0.7$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\lambda=1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$; $\lambda=0.7$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1][A1]; $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{7}{10} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\mathbf{s}_n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1]; $\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{3} \\ - \dfrac{11}{30} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $a_n=2\times\dfrac{1}{3}+(- \dfrac{11}{30})(0.7)^n$ [M1][A1]; $=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{11}{30}(0.7)^n$ [AG] [4 marks] (e) $\dfrac{11}{30}(0.7)^n\lt0.001$ [M1]; $n\gt16.55$ [A1]; $n=17$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) Revenue in month $k$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 12 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{s}_k=5+7a_k$ [M1][A1]; Sum over $k=0,\ldots,11$ of $5+7\left(\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{11}{30}(0.7)^k\right)$ [M1]; $\$107.56$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Diagonalize to get a closed form for $\mathbf{s}_n$. The dominant eigenvalue $1$ gives the steady state, and the other eigenvalue controls the speed of convergence.

subtopic: Rotation followed by a reflection in a line through the origin
statement: Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(2, 0)$, $B(0, 4)$ and $C(1, 1)$. (a) Write down the matrix $\mathbf{R}$ of the anticlockwise rotation through $90^\circ$ about the origin. [2] (b) The matrix of the reflection in the line $y=x\tan30^\circ$ is $\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$. Find the matrix $\mathbf{FR}$ of the rotation followed by the reflection. [3] (c) Find the image of the points $A(2, 0)$, $B(0, 4)$, $C(1, 1)$ under the combined transformation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos90^\circ & -\sin90^\circ \\ \sin90^\circ & \cos90^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{FR}$ (the first transformation is the right-hand matrix) [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2} \\ - \dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{FR}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ for each point [M1]; $A'=(\sqrt{3}, -1)$; $B'=(-2, - 2 \sqrt{3})$; $C'=(- \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2})$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply the matrices in order from right to left: $\mathbf{FR}\mathbf{v}$ means rotate first, then reflect.

subtopic: Composite of a rotation through 60 degrees and a reflection
statement: Triangle $PQR$ has vertices $P(4, 0)$, $Q(0, 2)$ and $R(2, 2)$. (a) Write down the matrix $\mathbf{R}$ of the anticlockwise rotation through $60^\circ$ about the origin. [2] (b) The matrix of the reflection in the line $y=x\tan45^\circ$ is $\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Find the matrix $\mathbf{FR}$ of the rotation followed by the reflection. [3] (c) Find the image of the points $P(4, 0)$, $Q(0, 2)$, $R(2, 2)$ under the combined transformation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos60^\circ & -\sin60^\circ \\ \sin60^\circ & \cos60^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{FR}$ (the first transformation is the right-hand matrix) [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{FR}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ for each point [M1]; $P'=(2 \sqrt{3}, 2)$; $Q'=(1, - \sqrt{3})$; $R'=(1 + \sqrt{3}, 1 - \sqrt{3})$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply the matrices in order from right to left: $\mathbf{FR}\mathbf{v}$ means rotate first, then reflect.

subtopic: Determinants, area scale factors and composite transformations
statement: Triangle $T$ has vertices $(1, 0)$, $(0, 2)$ and $(3, 1)$. The transformation $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is applied to $T$, giving triangle $T'$. Then the transformation $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is applied to $T'$, giving triangle $T''$. (a) Find the area of triangle $T$. [2] (b) Find the area of $T'$ and of $T''$. [4] (c) Find the single matrix that maps $T$ to $T''$, and describe the transformation $\mathbf{B}$ geometrically. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1}{2}\left|1(2-1)+0(1-0)+3(0-2)\right|$ [M1]; $\dfrac{5}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{A}=4$, so area of $T'=4\times\dfrac{5}{2}=10$ [M1][A1]; $\det\mathbf{B}=4$, so area of $T''=4\times10=40$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\mathbf{BA}=\begin{pmatrix} -4 & -4 \\ 6 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{B}=2\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$: an anticlockwise rotation through $90^\circ$ followed by an enlargement with scale factor $2$ (center the origin) [A1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: Area scale factor is the absolute value of the determinant. For composite transformations the determinants multiply.

subtopic: Finding a transformation matrix from two image points
statement: A linear transformation maps the point $(1, 1)$ to $(3, 5)$ and the point $(1, -1)$ to $(1, -1)$. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ of the transformation. [4] (b) Find the image of the point $(2, 3)$. [2] (c) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. State the area scale factor and whether the transformation preserves or reverses orientation. [3] (d) Find the point whose image is $(7, 11)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ where the columns are the given points and their images [M1]; $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\right)^{-1}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{M}=4$ [A1]; Area scale factor $=4$; positive determinant: orientation preserved [A1][R1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{3}{4} & - \dfrac{1}{4} \\ - \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $(\dfrac{5}{2}, 2)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The columns of a transformation matrix are the images of $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$. In general, write $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{I}_m$ and use $\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{I}_m\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.

subtopic: Matrix from two point-image pairs, determinant and inverse
statement: A linear transformation maps $(2, 1)$ to $(1, 8)$ and $(1, 2)$ to $(2, 7)$. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ of the transformation. [4] (b) Find the image of the point $(4, -3)$. [2] (c) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. State the area scale factor and whether the transformation preserves or reverses orientation. [3] (d) Find the point whose image is $(5, 9)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 8 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$ where the columns are the given points and their images [M1]; $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 8 & 7 \end{pmatrix}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\right)^{-1}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{M}=-3$ [A1]; Area scale factor $=3$; negative determinant: orientation reversed [A1][R1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $(- \dfrac{1}{3}, 5)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The columns of a transformation matrix are the images of $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$. In general, write $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{I}_m$ and use $\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{I}_m\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.

subtopic: Rotation followed by a stretch with a GDC
statement: A transformation consists of an anticlockwise rotation of $35^\circ$ about the origin, followed by a stretch with scale factor $2$ in the $x$-direction and scale factor $1.5$ in the $y$-direction. (a) Write down the matrix of the rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and of the stretch $\mathbf{S}$, and find the matrix $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{SR}$ of the rotation followed by the stretch. Give entries to $4$ significant figures. [4] (b) Find the image of the point $P(4, 3)$ under the transformation, to $3$ significant figures. [2] (c) The image of a point $X$ is $Q(5, 7)$. Find the coordinates of $X$ to $3$ significant figures. [3] (d) A region of area $7$ cm$^2$ is transformed. Find the area of its image. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8192 & -0.5736 \\ 0.5736 & 0.8192 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 1.638 & -1.147 \\ 0.8604 & 1.229 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $(3.11, 7.13)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $X=\mathbf{A}^{-1}Q$ (inverse on the GDC) [M1]; $(4.72, 2.39)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{A}=3.00$ [A1]; $3.00\times7=21.0$ cm$^2$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: The matrix of 'first $\mathbf{R}$ then $\mathbf{S}$' is $\mathbf{SR}$. The area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf{A}|$.

subtopic: Composite of a rotation through 120 degrees and a stretch
statement: A transformation consists of an anticlockwise rotation of $120^\circ$ about the origin, followed by a stretch with scale factor $0.8$ in the $x$-direction and scale factor $2$ in the $y$-direction. (a) Write down the matrix of the rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and of the stretch $\mathbf{S}$, and find the matrix $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{SR}$ of the rotation followed by the stretch. Give entries to $4$ significant figures. [4] (b) Find the image of the point $P(-3, 5)$ under the transformation, to $3$ significant figures. [2] (c) The image of a point $X$ is $Q(2, -4)$. Find the coordinates of $X$ to $3$ significant figures. [3] (d) A region of area $7$ cm$^2$ is transformed. Find the area of its image. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} -0.5000 & -0.8660 \\ 0.8660 & -0.5000 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} -0.4000 & -0.6928 \\ 1.732 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $(-2.26, -10.2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $X=\mathbf{A}^{-1}Q$ (inverse on the GDC) [M1]; $(-2.98, -1.17)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{A}=1.60$ [A1]; $1.60\times7=11.2$ cm$^2$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: The matrix of 'first $\mathbf{R}$ then $\mathbf{S}$' is $\mathbf{SR}$. The area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf{A}|$.

subtopic: Image of a quadrilateral, areas and the inverse matrix
statement: A transformation has matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. It is applied to the quadrilateral with vertices $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$, $C(5, 3)$ and $D(2, 4)$. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find the images of the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$. [3] (b) Find the area of the polygon and the area of its image. [4] (c) Find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ and the point whose image is $(7, 5)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ for each vertex [M1]; $A'=(3, 2)$; $B'=(9, -1)$; $C'=(13, 4)$; $D'=(8, 10)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=8$ [M1][A1]; $\det\mathbf{M}=7$, so image area $=7\times8=56$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{3}{7} & - \dfrac{1}{7} \\ \dfrac{1}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $(\dfrac{16}{7}, \dfrac{17}{7})$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area of the image is $|\det\mathbf{M}|$ times the original area. The inverse transformation undoes the original.

subtopic: Transforming a garden bed with a matrix
statement: A garden bed is modeled by the pentagon with vertices $P(0, 0)$, $Q(4, 0)$, $R(5, 2)$, $S(2, 4)$ and $T(-1, 2)$ (units in meters). The transformation $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is applied. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find the images of the vertices $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$. [3] (b) Find the area of the polygon and the area of its image. [4] (c) Find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ and the point whose image is $(11, 6)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ for each vertex [M1]; $P'=(0, 0)$; $Q'=(12, 0)$; $R'=(17, 4)$; $S'=(10, 8)$; $T'=(-1, 4)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=16$ [M1][A1]; $\det\mathbf{M}=6$, so image area $=6\times16=96$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{6} \\ 0 & \dfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $(\dfrac{8}{3}, 3)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area of the image is $|\det\mathbf{M}|$ times the original area. The inverse transformation undoes the original.

subtopic: Image of a line and a circle under a linear transformation
statement: The transformation $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is applied to the whole plane. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find the images of the points $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$, which lie on the line $l$ with equation $y=2x+1$. [3] (b) Hence find the equation of the image $l'$ of the line $l$ in the form $y=px+q$. [4] (c) The circle $C$ with radius $3$ and center the origin represents a circular pond. Find the area of the image of $C$ under $\mathbf{M}$, in terms of $\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{7-2}{5-1}=\dfrac{5}{4}$ [M1][A1]; $y=\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{3}{4}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{M}=3$ [A1]; Area $=3\times\pi\times3^2=27 \pi$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear transformation maps lines to lines. Use two points on the line to find the image line, and area scales by $|\det\mathbf{M}|$.

subtopic: Image of a line under a matrix and the effect on area
statement: A matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ transforms points of a plan of a park. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Find the images of the points $(0, -2)$ and $(1, -1)$, which lie on the line $l$ with equation $y=x-2$. [3] (b) Hence find the equation of the image $l'$ of the line $l$ in the form $y=px+q$. [4] (c) The circle $C$ with radius $4$ and center the origin represents a circular fountain. Find the area of the image of $C$ under $\mathbf{M}$, in terms of $\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{-1-(-4)}{4-2}=\dfrac{3}{2}$ [M1][A1]; $y=\dfrac{3}{2}x-7$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{M}=7$ [A1]; Area $=7\times\pi\times4^2=112 \pi$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear transformation maps lines to lines. Use two points on the line to find the image line, and area scales by $|\det\mathbf{M}|$.

subtopic: Scaling and shearing the corners of a photograph
statement: A photograph is a rectangle with corners $(0, 0)$, $(800, 0)$, $(800, 600)$ and $(0, 600)$ in pixels. An editing tool first scales the picture by a factor $1.25$ horizontally and $0.9$ vertically, and then applies a shear that maps $(x, y)$ to $(x+0.5y, y)$. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Write down the matrix $\mathbf{S}$ of the scaling, the matrix $\mathbf{H}$ of the shear, and the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ of the combined transformation. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the corners of the image. [3] (c) Find the area of the original picture and of the image, in square pixels. [3] (d) Explain why the shear alone does not change the area but the scaling does. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{5}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{9}{10} \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{HS}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{5}{4} & \dfrac{9}{20} \\ 0 & \dfrac{9}{10} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $(0, 0)$; $(1000, 0)$; $(1270, 540)$; $(270, 540)$ [M1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $800\times600=480000$ [A1]; $\det\mathbf{A}=\dfrac{9}{8}$, so image area $=\dfrac{9}{8}\times480000=540000$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{H}=1$ so area is unchanged by the shear; $\det\mathbf{S}=\dfrac{9}{8}\ne1$ so the scaling changes area [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The matrix for 'first $\mathbf{S}$ then $\mathbf{H}$' is $\mathbf{HS}$. A shear has determinant $1$.

subtopic: Repeated spiral transformations
statement: A design is built by repeatedly applying the transformation with matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ to the triangle $T_0$ with vertices $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$ and $(2, 1)$. The triangle $T_n$ is the image of $T_0$ under $\mathbf{M}^n$. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Show that $\mathbf{M}$ is a rotation through $45^\circ$ about the origin followed by an enlargement with center the origin, and state the scale factor. [3] (b) Find $\mathbf{M}^2$ and $\mathbf{M}^4$. [3] (c) Hence find $\mathbf{M}^8$ and describe the transformation it represents. [3] (d) Find the vertices of $T_1$ and the area of $T_0$, and hence the area of $T_n$ in terms of $n$. [4] (e) Find the smallest $n$ for which the area of $T_n$ exceeds $10000$. [3] (f) The reflection in the $x$-axis has matrix $\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Find the matrix $\mathbf{FM}$ and the image of the point $(2, 1)$ under $\mathbf{FM}$, and state the determinant of $\mathbf{FM}$ and its meaning for orientation. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}=\sqrt{2}\begin{pmatrix} \cos45^\circ & -\sin45^\circ \\ \sin45^\circ & \cos45^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ since $\cos45^\circ=\sin45^\circ=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ [M1][A1]; Rotation $45^\circ$ anticlockwise and enlargement with scale factor $\sqrt{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}^2=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $\mathbf{M}^4=\begin{pmatrix} -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{M}^8=\begin{pmatrix} 16 & 0 \\ 0 & 16 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; An enlargement with scale factor $16$, center the origin (no net rotation) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $T_1$: $(1, 1)$; $(-1, 1)$; $(1, 3)$ [A1]; Area of $T_0=1$ [A1]; $\det\mathbf{M}=2$, so area of $T_n=1\times2^n$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (e) $1\times2^n\gt10000$ [M1]; $n=14$ ($2^{13}\times1=8192$ and $2^{14}\times1=16384$) [A1][A1] [3 marks] (f) $\mathbf{FM}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; Image of $(2, 1)$ is $(1, -3)$ [A1]; $\det(\mathbf{FM})=-2$: area scale factor $2$ and orientation reversed [A1][R1] [5 marks]
tips: Powers of a spiral matrix rotate and enlarge: $\mathbf{M}^n$ rotates through $n\theta$ and enlarges by $k^n$. Area scales by $|\det\mathbf{M}|^n$.

subtopic: Three-variable system from ticket sales
statement: A cinema sells adult tickets for $\$a$, student tickets for $\$s$ and child tickets for $\$c$ each. On Monday it sold $4$ adult, $3$ student and $2$ child tickets for $\$62$. On Tuesday it sold $2$ adult, $5$ student and $3$ child tickets for $\$60$. On Wednesday it sold $3$ adult, $2$ student and $5$ child tickets for $\$59$. (a) Write the information as a system of three linear equations. [3] (b) Solve the system by elimination, showing your working. [6] (c) A group buys $2$ adult, $2$ student and $2$ child tickets. Find the total cost in dollars. [2]
markscheme: (a) $4a+3s+2c=62$, $2a+5s+3c=60$, $3a+2s+5c=59$ [A1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Eliminate $c$ from equations (1) and (2), and from equations (1) and (3): $8a-s=66$ and $14a+11s=192$ [M1][A1][A1]; Solve: $a=9$ and $s=6$ [M1][A1]; Substitute back: $c=4$ [A1] [6 marks] (c) $2a+2s+2c=\$38$ [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations, then solve the $2\times2$ system and back-substitute.

subtopic: A system from a jar of coins
statement: A jar holds $1$-cent, $5$-cent and $10$-cent coins. There are $30$ coins in total and their total value is $135$ cents. There are $5$ more $5$-cent coins than $1$-cent coins. Let $p$, $n$ and $d$ be the numbers of $1$-cent, $5$-cent and $10$-cent coins respectively. (a) Write the information as a system of three linear equations. [3] (b) Solve the system by elimination, showing your working. [6] (c) Find the total value, in cents, of all the $10$-cent coins in the jar. [2]
markscheme: (a) $p+n+d=30$, $p+5n+10d=135$, $-p+n=5$ [A1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Eliminate $d$ from equations (1) and (2), and from equations (1) and (3): $9p+5n=165$ and $p-n=-5$ [M1][A1][A1]; Solve: $p=10$ and $n=15$ [M1][A1]; Substitute back: $d=5$ [A1] [6 marks] (c) $10d=50$ cents [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations, then solve the $2\times2$ system and back-substitute.

subtopic: A three-equation system with a parameter: none or infinitely many
statement: Consider the system of equations with an unknown constant $k$. The system is: $-2x+3y+z=3$, $kx+3y+2z=2$, $2x+3y+kz=2$. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) For each of these values of $k$, determine whether the system has no solution or infinitely many solutions. [3] (c) For the value of $k$ with infinitely many solutions, find the general solution in terms of a parameter $t$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{A}=- 3 \left(k - 2\right) \left(k + 3\right)$ [M1][A1]; $k=-3$ or $k=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $k=-3$: reduce the augmented matrix; the system is inconsistent, so there is no solution [M1][A1]; $k=2$: the equations are dependent and consistent, so there are infinitely many solutions [A1] [3 marks] (c) Set $z=t$ and solve the remaining equations [M1][A1]; $(x, y, z)=\left(- \dfrac{t}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{t}{2}, t\right)$ [A1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: A system has a unique solution exactly when its coefficient matrix is invertible, that is $\det\mathbf{A}\ne0$. Where $\det\mathbf{A}=0$, check whether the augmented matrix is consistent.

subtopic: Unique, no or infinitely many solutions depending on k
statement: A system of three linear equations in $x$, $y$ and $z$ contains the parameter $k$. The system is: $-x+y+kz=3$, $kx+2y-z=0$, $y=1$. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) For each of these values of $k$, determine whether the system has no solution or infinitely many solutions. [3] (c) For the value of $k$ with infinitely many solutions, find the general solution in terms of a parameter $t$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{A}=\left(k - 1\right) \left(k + 1\right)$ [M1][A1]; $k=-1$ or $k=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $k=-1$: reduce the augmented matrix; the system is inconsistent, so there is no solution [M1][A1]; $k=1$: the equations are dependent and consistent, so there are infinitely many solutions [A1] [3 marks] (c) Set $z=t$ and solve the remaining equations [M1][A1]; $(x, y, z)=\left(t - 2, 1, t\right)$ [A1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: A system has a unique solution exactly when its coefficient matrix is invertible, that is $\det\mathbf{A}\ne0$. Where $\det\mathbf{A}=0$, check whether the augmented matrix is consistent.

subtopic: Mixing two nut types by cost and mass
statement: A shop mixes almonds costing $\$12$ per kilogram with cashews costing $\$18$ per kilogram to make $20$ kg of a mix that costs $\$15.60$ per kilogram on average, so the total cost is $\$312$. Let $x$ be the mass of almonds and $y$ the mass of cashews, both in kilograms. (a) Form two equations and solve them to find $x$ and $y$. [5] (b) Find the cost of the almonds used, in dollars. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x+y=20$ and $12x+18y=312$ [A1][A1]; Eliminate one variable between the two equations (for example by substitution) [M1]; $x=8$, $y=12$ [A1][A1] [5 marks] (b) $12x=\$96$ [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Name the two unknowns, write one equation for each piece of information, and eliminate.

subtopic: A cubic model through four points for shop profit
statement: A shop records its weekly profit $P$ (in thousands of dollars) at four advertising budgets $x$ (in thousands of dollars): $(1, 3.2)$, $(2, 6.9)$, $(4, 12.1)$ and $(5, 11.5)$. The profit is modeled by a cubic function of $x$. Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Write down a system of 4 equations for the coefficients $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, and solve it on your GDC. [4] (b) Hence write down the model and use it to estimate the profit when the budget is $3$ thousand dollars. [2] (c) Use the model to find the greatest value of the profit for $1\le x\le7$ and the budget at which it occurs. [3] (d) Find the first value of the budget in this range for which the model gives a profit of $10$ thousand dollars. [2]
markscheme: (a) $3.2=a(1^3)+b(1^2)+c(1)+d$; $6.9=a(2^3)+b(2^2)+c(2)+d$; $12.1=a(4^3)+b(4^2)+c(4)+d$; $11.5=a(5^3)+b(5^2)+c(5)+d$ [A1][A1]; Matrix solution: $a=-0.175$, $b=0.858$, $c=2.35$, $d=0.167$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $P=-0.175x^3+0.858x^2+2.35x+0.167$ [A1]; $P=10.2$ thousand dollars [A1] [2 marks] (c) Maximum of the graph on the GDC [M1]; budget $=4.31$ thousand dollars and profit $=12.2$ thousand dollars [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $-0.175x^3+0.858x^2+2.35x+0.167=10$ on the GDC [M1]; budget $=2.92$ thousand dollars [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute each point into the model to get linear equations in the coefficients, then solve with the inverse matrix on the GDC.

subtopic: Diet planning with three foods
statement: A nutritionist mixes three foods $F_1$, $F_2$ and $F_3$. Per $100$ g, the foods contain the following grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat, collected in the matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 12 & 5 & 20 \\ 20 & 40 & 5 \\ 4 & 12 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ (rows: protein, carbohydrate, fat; columns: $F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$). The daily targets are $57.5$ g of protein, $115$ g of carbohydrate and $36$ g of fat. Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the amounts, in units of $100$ g, of $F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$ needed to meet the targets exactly. (a) Write the situation as a matrix equation $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, stating $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to solve the system. [4] (c) The cost per 100 g of the three items is $\$1.2$, $\$0.8$ and $\$1.5$ respectively. Find the total cost. [2] (d) The new daily targets are $40$ g of protein, $100$ g of carbohydrate and $30$ g of fat. Use the same matrix $\mathbf{A}$ to decide whether the new requirements can be met with non-negative amounts, giving your reason. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 57.5 \\ 115 \\ 36 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=2.5$, $y=1.5$, $z=1$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $1.2\times2.5+0.8\times1.5+1.5\times1$ [M1]; $\$5.70$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_{new}=\begin{pmatrix} 1.78 \\ 1.54 \\ 0.547 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; All entries are non-negative, so the requirement can be met [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A system with the same matrix and different right-hand side only needs the same inverse. Negative amounts are impossible in context.

subtopic: Production planning with three machines
statement: A factory makes three products $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$. The matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ gives the hours needed on machines $M_1$, $M_2$ and $M_3$ (rows) for one unit of each product (columns). The machines have $85$, $85$ and $100$ hours available per week and all of the time is used. Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the weekly numbers of units of $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$. Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Write the situation as a matrix equation $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, stating $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to solve the system. [4] (c) The cost per unit of the three items is $\$14$, $\$9$ and $\$11$ respectively. Find the total cost. [2] (d) In a different week the available hours are $120$ on $M_1$, $60$ on $M_2$ and $100$ on $M_3$. Use the same matrix $\mathbf{A}$ to decide whether the new requirements can be met with non-negative amounts, giving your reason. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 85 \\ 85 \\ 100 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=20$, $y=15$, $z=10$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $14\times20+9\times15+11\times10$ [M1]; $\$525.00$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_{new}=\begin{pmatrix} 28.9 \\ -4.44 \\ 22.2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; One entry is negative, so the requirement cannot be met [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A system with the same matrix and different right-hand side only needs the same inverse. Negative amounts are impossible in context.

subtopic: Fertilizer mix for nutrient targets
statement: A farmer blends three fertilizers $F_1$, $F_2$ and $F_3$. The matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 20 & 5 \\ 5 & 10 & 25 \\ 10 & 5 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ gives the percentage by mass of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (rows) in each fertilizer (columns). The mixture must supply exactly $11$ kg of nitrogen, $10$ kg of phosphorus and $6.5$ kg of potassium. Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the masses in kg of $F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$ used. (a) Write the situation as a matrix equation $\dfrac{1}{100}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, stating $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to solve the system. [4] (c) The cost per kilogram of the three items is $\$0.9$, $\$1.1$ and $\$1.4$ respectively. Find the total cost. [2] (d) A different field needs $8$ kg of nitrogen, $14$ kg of phosphorus and $4$ kg of potassium. Use the same matrix $\mathbf{A}$ to decide whether the new requirements can be met with non-negative amounts, giving your reason. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 11 \\ 10 \\ 6.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{x}=\left(\dfrac{1}{100}\mathbf{A}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=40$, $y=30$, $z=20$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $0.9\times40+1.1\times30+1.4\times20$ [M1]; $\$97.00$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_{new}=\begin{pmatrix} 4.44 \\ 26.7 \\ 44.4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; All entries are non-negative, so the requirement can be met [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A system with the same matrix and different right-hand side only needs the same inverse. Negative amounts are impossible in context.

subtopic: Investment portfolio across three funds
statement: A fund manager invests a total of $\$20000$ in three funds paying annual interest of $3\%$, $5\%$ and $8\%$, with amounts $\$x$, $\$y$ and $\$z$ respectively. The total interest after one year is $\$1080$. The amount in the first fund is twice the amount in the second fund. Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Form three linear equations in $x$, $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Solve the system on your GDC. [4] (c) Find the interest earned from each fund in the year, and state which fund earns the most. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x+y+z=20000$ [A1]; $0.03x+0.05y+0.08z=1080$ [A1]; $x-2y=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Matrix inverse or polynomial solver [M1]; $x=8000$, $y=4000$, $z=8000$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $240$, $200$, $640$ [M1][A1]; Fund 3 earns the most [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set up one equation for the total invested, one for the total interest, and one for the extra condition, then solve with a matrix inverse.

subtopic: Splitting a savings pot between three accounts
statement: A saver splits $\$15000$ between three accounts paying $2.5\%$, $4\%$ and $6\%$ per year, with amounts $\$x$, $\$y$ and $\$z$. After one year the total interest is $\$610$. The amount in the third account is $\$1000$ less than in the first. Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Form three linear equations in $x$, $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Solve the system on your GDC. [4] (c) Find the interest earned from each fund in the year, and state which fund earns the most. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x+y+z=15000$ [A1]; $0.025x+0.04y+0.06z=610$ [A1]; $x-z=1000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Matrix inverse or polynomial solver [M1]; $x=6000$, $y=4000$, $z=5000$ [A1][A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $150$, $160$, $300$ [M1][A1]; Fund 3 earns the most [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set up one equation for the total invested, one for the total interest, and one for the extra condition, then solve with a matrix inverse.

subtopic: Z-interval for a mean with known standard deviation (by hand)
statement: The masses of jars of honey are normally distributed with known standard deviation $\sigma=8$ g. A random sample of $64$ jars has a mean mass of $\bar x=502$ g. (a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. [2] (b) Find the margin of error and hence the 95\% confidence interval for $\mu$. Use $z=1.96$. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the interval would be wider or narrower for a 99\% confidence level using the same data. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{64}}=1$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) Margin of error $=1.96\times1=1.96$ [M1][A1]; $\left(500.04, 503.96\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Wider: a higher confidence level needs a larger critical value, so a larger margin [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A confidence interval for a mean with known $\sigma$ is $\bar x\pm z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.

subtopic: Confidence interval for the mean time of a computer task
statement: The time taken by a computer to complete a task is normally distributed with standard deviation $\sigma=3$ seconds. In $36$ runs the mean time was $\bar x=24$ seconds. (a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. [2] (b) Find the margin of error and hence the 90\% confidence interval for $\mu$. Use $z=1.645$. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the interval would be wider or narrower for a 99\% confidence level using the same data. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{36}}=0.5$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) Margin of error $=1.645\times0.5=0.8225$ [M1][A1]; $\left(23.1775, 24.8225\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Wider: a higher confidence level needs a larger critical value, so a larger margin [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A confidence interval for a mean with known $\sigma$ is $\bar x\pm z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.

subtopic: Recovering the mean and standard deviation from a confidence interval
statement: A $95\%$ confidence interval for a population mean was constructed from a random sample of size $100$, using $z=1.96$ and a known population standard deviation $\sigma$. The interval is $(37.06, 42.94)$. (a) Find the sample mean. [2] (b) Find the margin of error. [2] (c) Hence find the population standard deviation $\sigma$ that was used. [3]
tips: The center of the interval is the sample mean and half its width is the margin of error $z\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

subtopic: Working backwards from an interval to sigma
statement: A $90\%$ confidence interval for a population mean was calculated from a random sample of size $25$, using $z=1.645$ and a known population standard deviation $\sigma$. The interval is $(18.355, 21.645)$. (a) Find the sample mean. [2] (b) Find the margin of error. [2] (c) Hence find the population standard deviation $\sigma$ that was used. [3]
tips: The center of the interval is the sample mean and half its width is the margin of error $z\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

subtopic: Sample size for a given margin of error
statement: A researcher estimates the mean reaction time of drivers. The population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma=0.6$ seconds. (a) Write down an inequality for $n$ so that the margin of error of a 95\% confidence interval is at most $0.12$. Use $z=1.96$. [2] (b) Find the smallest sample size $n$. [3] (c) Explain why halving the margin of error requires about four times as many observations. [1]
markscheme: (a) $1.96\times\dfrac{0.6}{\sqrt{n}}\le0.12$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sqrt{n}\ge\dfrac{1.96\times0.6}{0.12}=9.8$ [M1]; $n\ge96.04$, so $n=97$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) The margin of error is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, so halving it requires $\sqrt{n}$ to double, which multiplies $n$ by $4$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The margin of error is $z\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Solve for $n$ and round up.

subtopic: T-interval from raw data
statement: A baker weighs $10$ loaves of bread (in grams), chosen at random. The values are: 498, 505, 492, 510, 503, 495, 507, 500, 496, 509. Assume that the population is normally distributed. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation, each to $4$ significant figures. [2] (b) Find the 95\% confidence interval for the mean mass of a loaf, giving the endpoints to $4$ significant figures. [4] (c) A specification claims that the population mean is 500 g. State whether your interval supports this claim. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=501.5$ [A1]; $s_{n-1}=6.241$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t_{9}$ critical value $=2.262$ (GDC inverse $t$ or $t$-interval function) [M1][A1]; $\bar x\pm t\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=501.5\pm4.464$ [M1]; $\left(497.0, 506.0\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The interval contains 500, so the claim is consistent with the data [R1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom because $\sigma$ is unknown. The GDC $t$-interval function gives the endpoints directly.

subtopic: Confidence interval for a mean battery life from a small sample
statement: The lifetimes (in hours) of $9$ randomly chosen batteries of one brand are measured. The values are: 41.2, 39.8, 43.5, 38.9, 40.7, 42.1, 44, 37.6, 40.3. Assume that the population is normally distributed. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation, each to $4$ significant figures. [2] (b) Find the 99\% confidence interval for the mean lifetime of a battery, giving the endpoints to $4$ significant figures. [4] (c) A specification claims that the population mean is 45 hours. State whether your interval supports this claim. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=40.90$ [A1]; $s_{n-1}=2.074$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t_{8}$ critical value $=3.355$ (GDC inverse $t$ or $t$-interval function) [M1][A1]; $\bar x\pm t\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=40.90\pm2.319$ [M1]; $\left(38.58, 43.22\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The interval does not contain 45, so the data do not support the claim at this confidence level [R1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom because $\sigma$ is unknown. The GDC $t$-interval function gives the endpoints directly.

subtopic: T-intervals from summary statistics and comparing confidence levels
statement: A random sample of $n=16$ bolts has mean length $\bar x=52.4$ mm and sample standard deviation $s=1.8$ mm (unbiased estimate). The lengths are normally distributed. (a) Find the 90\% confidence interval for $\mu$, giving the endpoints to $4$ significant figures. [4] (b) Find the 99\% confidence interval and state its width. Compare the width with that of the 90\% interval. [3] (c) The population standard deviation is later found to be exactly $1.8$ mm. Find the corresponding $90\%$ $z$-interval and explain why it is narrower than the $t$-interval. [3]
markscheme: (a) $t_{15}=1.753$ [M1][A1]; $52.4\pm1.753\times\dfrac{1.8}{\sqrt{16}}$ [M1]; $\left(51.61, 53.19\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left(51.07, 53.73\right)$ [A1]; Width $=2.652$ compared with 1.578: the 99\% interval is wider [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=1.645$; $\left(51.66, 53.14\right)$ [M1][A1]; The $z$ critical value is smaller than the $t$ critical value (the $t$ distribution has heavier tails because $s$ is itself estimated from a small sample) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A $t$-interval is wider than the corresponding $z$-interval for the same $s$ and $n$ because the $t$-distribution has heavier tails.

subtopic: Confidence interval for a mean difference with paired data
statement: Eight athletes record their resting heart rate (in beats per minute) before and after a $6$-week training program. Before: 68, 72, 75, 64, 80, 70, 66, 74. After: 64, 70, 71, 63, 74, 69, 62, 70. Assume the differences are normally distributed. Give non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Calculate the difference $d=\text{after}-\text{before}$ for each athlete, and find the mean and the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation of the differences. [3] (b) Find the 95\% confidence interval for the mean difference $\mu_d$. [3] (c) Interpret the interval in terms of whether there was a change on average. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d$: -4, -2, -4, -1, -6, -1, -4, -4 [A1]; $\bar d=-3.250$, $s_{n-1}=1.753$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $t_{7}=2.365$ [M1][A1]; $\left(-4.715, -1.785\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The interval lies entirely below $0$, so the data suggest a decrease on average [R1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: For paired data, work with the differences and use a $t$-interval on them.

subtopic: Comparing two groups using confidence intervals
statement: Two methods of teaching a skill are compared. Scores on a final test are normally distributed in both groups. Method $A$: $n=15$ students, mean $72.4$, sample standard deviation $6.1$ (unbiased estimate). Method $B$: $n=20$ students, mean $78.9$, sample standard deviation $8.2$ (unbiased estimate). (a) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean score under each method, with endpoints to $3$ significant figures. [4] (b) State whether the two intervals overlap, and what, if anything, this tells you about the difference in the population means. [2] (c) Method $B$ students are also given a second test. The mean of their differences (second $-$ first) is $3.1$ with standard deviation of differences $4.4$ for the $20$ students. Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean difference. [3] (d) Does your interval from part (c) suggest that scores improved on average? Justify your answer. [1] (e) State two assumptions made when constructing the intervals above. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A$: $t_{14}=2.145$, $\left(69.0, 75.8\right)$ [M1][A1]; $B$: $t_{19}=2.093$, $\left(75.1, 82.7\right)$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) The intervals overlap, so we cannot conclude from this alone that the population means differ [A1]; Overlap of two separate intervals is not a formal test; a correct comparison would use an interval for the difference in means [R1] [2 marks] (c) $3.1\pm2.093\times\dfrac{4.4}{\sqrt{20}}$ [M1][A1]; $\left(1.04, 5.16\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The interval is entirely above $0$, so there is evidence of an average improvement [R1] [1 mark] (e) The populations are normal (or the samples are random and large enough); the samples are random (and independent where compared) [A1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Overlapping intervals do not prove that two population means are equal. Use $t$-intervals when $\sigma$ is unknown.

subtopic: Quality control of cereal boxes using confidence intervals
statement: A factory fills boxes of cereal with a target mean mass of $500$ g. A quality inspector weighs $15$ randomly chosen boxes (in grams): 502.1, 498.7, 505.3, 500.4, 497.9, 503.6, 499.2, 501.8, 504.4, 496.5, 500.9, 502.7, 498.1, 503.2, 499.8. Assume the masses are normally distributed. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation, each to $4$ significant figures. [2] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean mass, with endpoints to $4$ significant figures, and state whether the target mean of $500$ g lies in it. [5] (c) Find the corresponding $99\%$ confidence interval and explain why it is wider. [4] (d) The company wants a $95\%$ interval with margin of error at most $1$ g. Treating $s$ as the population standard deviation, find the sample size needed. [3] (e) Each week the inspector constructs a new $95\%$ confidence interval from a new random sample. Over $20$ weeks, find the expected number of intervals that contain the true mean, and the probability that at least $18$ of them do. Assume the intervals are independent. [4] (f) Find the probability that all $20$ intervals contain the true mean, and comment on what this shows about the meaning of $95\%$ confidence. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=501.0$ [A1]; $s_{n-1}=2.605$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t_{14}=2.145$ [A1]; Margin $=2.145\times\dfrac{2.605}{\sqrt{15}}=1.442$ [M1][A1]; $\left(499.5, 502.4\right)$; $500$ lies inside [A1][A1] [5 marks] (c) $t_{14}=2.977$, margin $=2.002$; $\left(499.0, 503.0\right)$ [M1][A1][A1]; A higher confidence level requires a larger critical value, so a larger margin of error [R1] [4 marks] (d) $1.96\times\dfrac{2.605}{\sqrt{n}}\le1$ [M1]; $n\ge26.06$, so $n=27$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (e) $X\sim B(20, 0.95)$, $E(X)=19$ [M1][A1]; $P(X\ge18)=1-P(X\le17)=0.9245$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (f) $0.95^{20}=0.358$ [A1]; Even if the process is unchanged, there is a substantial chance that at least one interval misses the true mean: $95\%$ refers to the long-run proportion of intervals that capture the mean, not to any single interval [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $t$-intervals when $\sigma$ is unknown. The confidence level is the long-run proportion of intervals that capture the true mean.

subtopic: Best-of-five series between two teams
statement: Teams $A$ and $B$ play a series of games. The first team to win $3$ games wins the series, so at most $5$ games are played. Each game is won by team $A$ with probability $0.6$ and by team $B$ with probability $0.4$, independently of other games. Give exact values or answers correct to $4$ significant figures. (a) Find the probability that team $A$ wins the series in exactly $4$ games. [3] (b) Show that the probability that the series lasts exactly $5$ games is $0.3456$. [2] (c) Find the probability that team $A$ wins the series. [3] (d) Let $N$ be the number of games played. Find the probability distribution of $N$ and hence $E(N)$. [6] (e) Given that the series lasts exactly $5$ games, find the probability that team $A$ wins it, and explain why this equals $0.6$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A$ wins game $4$ and exactly $2$ of the first $3$ games [M1]; $\binom{3}{2}(0.6)^2(0.4)\times0.6=0.2592$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) After $4$ games each team has won $2$ games: $\binom{4}{2}(0.6)^2(0.4)^2$ [M1][A1]; $6\times0.36\times0.16=0.3456$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $P(A\text{ in }3)+P(A\text{ in }4)+P(A\text{ in }5)$ [M1]; $0.216+0.2592+0.20736$ [A1]; $=0.68256$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $P(N=3)=0.6^3+0.4^3=0.28$ [A1]; $P(N=4)=3(0.6)^3(0.4)+3(0.4)^3(0.6)=0.3744$ [M1][A1]; $P(N=5)=0.3456$ [A1]; $E(N)=3(0.28)+4(0.3744)+5(0.3456)=4.066$ [M1][A1] [6 marks] (e) $\dfrac{6(0.6)^3(0.4)^2}{0.3456}=0.6$ [M1][A1]; After $4$ games the score is $2$–$2$ whatever the order; the series is then decided by the fifth game, which $A$ wins with probability $0.6$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: List the ways a series can end: the winner always wins the last game. Use $\binom{n}{k}$ for the order of earlier wins.

subtopic: Screening test: Bayes' theorem and repeated tests
statement: A disease affects $2\%$ of a population. A screening test gives a positive result for $95\%$ of people who have the disease and for $10\%$ of people who do not have the disease. When a test is repeated on the same person, the results are independent given whether the person has the disease. Let $D$ be the event that a person has the disease. (a) A person is chosen at random and tested once. Find the probability that the result is positive. [3] (b) Given that the first test is positive, find the probability that the person has the disease. Give your answer to $3$ significant figures. [3] (c) A person with a positive first result is tested a second time and the second result is also positive. Find the probability that the person has the disease. [3] (d) A person is declared to have the disease only if $k$ consecutive tests are all positive. Find the smallest $k$ for which the probability that a person so declared has the disease exceeds $0.99$. [3] (e) Each first test costs $\$4$. Anyone with a positive first result has a second test, which costs $\$12$. Find the expected total cost per person screened. [3] (f) Under this two-test policy a person is declared positive only if both tests are positive. Find the probability that a randomly chosen person is classified correctly. [3]
tips: Draw a tree: first branch disease status, then test results. Independence is conditional on disease status, so multiply along branches.

subtopic: Suspension cable modeled by a quadratic
statement: The height $h$ meters above the road of a suspension cable at horizontal distance $x$ meters from the left tower is modeled by $h=a(x-20)^2+2$. The cable is attached to the left tower at height $10$ m, at $x=0$. (a) Find the value of $a$. [2] (b) Find the height of the cable at $x=5$. [2] (c) Find the two values of $x$ at which the cable is $4$ m above the road. [3]
tips: The vertex form $a(x-h)^2+k$ shows the lowest point at $(h, k)$.

subtopic: Aircraft on a landing approach
statement: An aircraft on its approach has position, in meters relative to a point $O$ on the runway level, $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} -2400 \\ 300 \\ 450 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 60 \\ -5 \\ -9 \end{pmatrix}$ where $t$ is in seconds and $z$ is the height above the runway. (a) Find the speed of the aircraft, to $3$ significant figures. [2] (b) Find the time at which the aircraft reaches a height of $200$ m, and its position then. [3] (c) The aircraft continues until it lands (when $z=0$). Find the position where it lands and the horizontal distance traveled from the start, to $3$ significant figures. [5] (d) Find the angle between the path of the aircraft and the horizontal ground, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{60^2+(-5)^2+(-9)^2}$ [M1]; $60.9$ m per second [A1] [2 marks] (b) $450+(-9)t=200$ [M1]; $t=27.8$ [A1]; Position $=\begin{pmatrix} -733.3 \\ 161.1 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=0$ gives $t=50$ [M1][A1]; Landing point $=\begin{pmatrix} 600 \\ 50 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; Horizontal distance $=\sqrt{3000^2+(-250)^2}=3010$ m [M1][A1] [5 marks] (d) $\sin\phi=\dfrac{9}{60.88}$ (vertical component over speed) [M1][A1]; $\phi=8.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The $z$ coordinate gives height. The angle with the ground is found from the vertical component of the velocity.

subtopic: Comparing two cost plans and break-even
statement: A printing shop offers two ways to produce posters. Option A has a set-up fee of $\$120$ and $\$0.80$ per poster. Option B has a set-up fee of $\$40$ and $\$1.30$ per poster. Costs are in dollars. Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Write down a linear function for the total cost of each option for $n$ posters. [2] (b) Find the number of posters for which the two options cost the same, and the common cost. [3] (c) State which option is cheaper for 200 posters, with a reason. [2] (d) The shop sells each poster for $\$2.50$. Using option A, find the smallest whole number of posters that must be sold for the income to exceed the cost. [3]
tips: The break-even point is where two linear costs are equal. 'Exceed' requires a strict inequality, so round up to the next whole number.

subtopic: Hire cost comparison with a break-even point
statement: A company can hire a van from firm $A$ for a fixed charge of $\$75$ plus $\$0.45$ per kilometer, or from firm $B$ for a fixed charge of $\$30$ plus $\$0.70$ per kilometer. Costs are in dollars. Give money values to the nearest cent and other non-exact answers correct to $3$ significant figures. (a) Write down a linear function for the total cost of each option for $n$ kilometers. [2] (b) Find the number of kilometers for which the two options cost the same, and the common cost. [3] (c) State which option is cheaper for 150 kilometers, with a reason. [2] (d) The company charges its customers $\$1.20$ per kilometer driven. Using firm $A$, find the smallest whole number of kilometers for which the income exceeds the cost. [3]
tips: The break-even point is where two linear costs are equal. 'Exceed' requires a strict inequality, so round up to the next whole number.
